sk: तदेतत्सत्यं मन्त्रेषु कर्माणि कवयो यान्यपश्यंस्तानि त्रेतायां बहुधा सन्ततानि तान्याचरथ नियतं सत्यकामा एष वः पन्थाः सुकृतस्य लोके ||
ro: tat · etat · satyam · mantreṣu · karmāṇi · kavayaḥ · yāni · apaśyan · tāni · tretāyāṁ · bahudhā · santatāni · tāni · ācaratha · niyataṁ · satya-kāmāḥ · eṣaḥ · vaḥ · panthāḥ · sukṛtasya · loke ||
hi: वह यह सत्य है — मन्त्रों में कवियों (ऋषियों) ने जो कर्म (यज्ञ-कर्म) देखे — वे त्रेता (तीन अग्नियों वाले यज्ञ) में बहुधा (बहुत प्रकार से) विस्तारित (सन्ततानि) हैं। हे सत्यकाम (सत्य की इच्छा रखने वाले) पुरुषो! उन कर्मों को नियमपूर्वक (नियतम्) आचरण करो — यह तुम्हारा सुकृत-लोक (पुण्य-लोक) का मार्ग (पन्थाः) है।
en: This is the truth: the ritual actions (karmāṇi) that the sages (kavayaḥ) saw in the mantras are spread in many ways (bahudhā santatāni) across the three sacrificial fires (tretāyām). Perform them diligently (niyatam), O lovers of truth (satya-kāmāḥ)! This is your path (panthāḥ) to the world of good deeds (sukṛtasya loke).

ws.e: sages / seers — those who 'saw' (apaśyan) the ritual actions in the Vedic mantras; kavi here = ṛṣi, the original receivers of Vedic revelation
ritual actions — the sacrificial rites prescribed by the Vedas; the plural indicates the great variety of Vedic rituals
in the three fires — tretā = triad; the three Vedic sacrificial fires: gārhapatya (householder's fire), āhavanīya (offering fire), dakṣiṇāgni (southern fire)
spread out / extended — from √tan (to stretch); the rituals are elaborately spread across the three fires in many forms
lovers of truth / those who desire the true — satya (truth) + kāma (desire); an epithet for earnest seekers

ws.h: सुकृत (पुण्य) के लोक में / पुण्य-लोक में
ws.e: in the world of merit — sukṛta (well-done/meritorious) + loka (world); the heavenly realm earned through good deeds and proper ritual

gr: The ritual path introduced: the Muṇḍaka now turns to aparā vidyā in action — the path of ritual (karma-mārga). This mantra endorses the ritual path: it is 'satya' (true), it was 'seen' by the seers, and it leads to sukṛta-loka (the world of merit). tretāyām — 'in the three fires': the tretāgni (three sacred fires) are the foundation of Vedic ritual: (1) gārhapatya — the householder's fire, always burning, source of all other fires; (2) āhavanīya — the offering fire, into which oblations are poured; (3) dakṣiṇāgni — the southern fire, associated with the ancestors. The ambiguity: the mantra says 'this is your path to the world of good deeds' — not 'this is your path to liberation (mokṣa).' The destination is sukṛta-loka — a heavenly reward — not the Imperishable (akṣara). This is the beginning of the Muṇḍaka's critique: rituals work, but they don't take you to the ultimate goal.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.1 — This mantra begins the Muṇḍaka's famous critique of the ritual path (karma-kāṇḍa). The section (1.2.1-13) first presents the ritualistic religion sympathetically (mantras 1-6) and then delivers a devastating critique (mantras 7-13). The tretāgni (three fires) system is central to Śrauta ritual — the elaborate Vedic sacrifices described in the Brāhmaṇa texts. The phrase 'sukṛtasya loke' (world of merit) is significant — it explicitly limits the ritual path's destination to heaven, not to Brahman.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — यह मन्त्र अपरा विद्या (कर्मकाण्ड) का वर्णन प्रारम्भ करता है। 'सुकृतस्य लोके' — कर्मकाण्ड का फल स्वर्ग-लोक (heaven) है — मोक्ष (liberation) नहीं। कर्म 'सत्य' है — अर्थात् फलदायी (fruit-giving) है — किन्तु अनित्य फल (impermanent fruit) देता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says this mantra begins the description of aparā vidyā (karma-kāṇḍa) in action. 'Sukṛtasya loke' — the fruit of ritual is heaven — not liberation. Karma is 'satya' (true) — meaning it is effective/fruit-giving — but its fruit is impermanent.
advaita.ins: The Upanishad is fair: rituals work. They're not false. They deliver exactly what they promise — a better world. But 'a better world' is not the same as 'the Imperishable.' Heaven is a place; Brahman is not a place. That's the gap this section will expose.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — कर्मकाण्ड भगवान् की आराधना (worship) का एक वैध (valid) मार्ग है। 'सत्यम्' = यह सत्य मार्ग है — किन्तु यह एकमात्र मार्ग नहीं है। 'सुकृतस्य लोके' = भगवान् के लोक (divine realm) में — भक्ति से जुड़े कर्म भगवत्-प्राप्ति का साधन बन सकते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says karma-kāṇḍa is a valid path of worshipping the Lord. 'Satya' = it is a true path — but not the only path. 'Sukṛtasya loke' = in the Lord's realm — rituals combined with devotion can become a means to reach the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Rituals are a conversation with God — through fire, through offering, through discipline. The conversation is real. But if you only talk TO God and never listen for God talking back — you'll stay on the surface of the relationship.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — मन्त्रों में 'देखे गये' कर्म = चेतना के बाह्य अनुष्ठान (external rituals of consciousness)। ये 'सत्य' हैं — किन्तु चेतना के बाह्य स्तर (outer level) पर। आन्तरिक यज्ञ (inner sacrifice) = परा विद्या। बाह्य यज्ञ = अपरा विद्या।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the actions 'seen' in mantras = external rituals of consciousness. They are 'satya' — but at the outer level of consciousness. The inner sacrifice = parā vidyā. The outer sacrifice = aparā vidyā.
aurobindo.ins: The ancient seers didn't invent rituals arbitrarily — they saw them. They perceived patterns in consciousness and translated them into actions with fire, milk, and ghee. The rituals are real maps of real processes. But a map of the ocean is not the ocean.

dp.q: 🔍 The three sacrificial fires (tretāgni)
dp.a: The tretāgni — the three sacred fires — are the foundation of Vedic Śrauta (solemn) ritual: The three fires: (1) Gārhapatya (गार्हपत्य) — the 'householder's fire,' always kept burning in the home; it is the 'mother fire' from which the other two are kindled; round in shape, placed to the west. (2) Āhavanīya (आहवनीय) — the 'offering fire,' into which oblations (havis) are poured during sacrifice; square in shape, placed to the east; it is the 'mouth of the gods.' (3) Dakṣiṇāgni (दक्षिणाग्नि) — the 'southern fire,' associated with the ancestors (pitṛs) and with protection against evil; semicircular in shape, placed to the south. How they function: in a Vedic sacrifice (yajña), the three fires form a ritual arena. The gārhapatya is the source; the āhavanīya receives offerings to the gods; the dakṣiṇāgni protects and connects to the ancestral realm. Offerings of ghee, milk, soma, grain, and other substances are poured into the fires while Vedic mantras are chanted. Why the Muṇḍaka mentions them: the tretāgni system represents the full apparatus of Vedic ritual — not just domestic worship but the elaborate, expensive, multi-priest Śrauta ceremonies. The Muṇḍaka acknowledges their validity ('satya') before critiquing their sufficiency (mantras 7-13).

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the Muṇḍaka first endorse rituals before critiquing them?
dp.a: The Muṇḍaka's rhetorical strategy is deliberate: first present the ritual path sympathetically (1.2.1-6), then deliver the critique (1.2.7-13). Why not just reject rituals outright? (1) Respect for tradition: the audience (Śaunaka and his circle) are learned householders steeped in Vedic ritual. Dismissing their entire way of life without acknowledgment would be counterproductive. (2) Intellectual honesty: the ritual path does work — it produces real results (heavenly rewards, prosperity, social order). Denying this would be false. (3) Pedagogical progression: the student must understand what is being transcended before being told to transcend it. You can't go 'beyond' something you don't understand. (4) The critique is about sufficiency, not validity: the Muṇḍaka's argument is not 'rituals are false' but 'rituals are insufficient.' They deliver what they promise (sukṛta-loka) but they cannot deliver what they don't promise (the Imperishable). The parallel: this is the same strategy used in the Bhagavad Gītā (2.42-46), where Kṛṣṇa first describes those who are attached to Vedic rituals ('flowery speech of the unwise') and then says 'the Vedas deal with the three guṇas; be free of the three guṇas.' Acknowledge, then transcend.

sk: यदा लेलायते ह्यर्चिः समिद्धे हव्यवाहने तदाज्यभागावन्तरेणाहुतीः प्रतिपादयेत् ||
ro: yadā · lelāyate · hi · arciḥ · samiddhe · havya-vāhane · tadā · ājya-bhāgau · antareṇa · āhutīḥ · pratipādayet ||
hi: जब अग्नि (हव्यवाहन — oblation-carrier) समिद्ध (well-kindled / प्रज्ज्वलित) हो और ज्वाला (अर्चिः) लेलायते (लहराती / चमकती) हो — तब दो आज्यभागों (घृत-आहुतियों / ghee-oblations) के बीच में (अन्तरेण) आहुतियाँ (offerings) प्रतिपादयेत् (प्रदान करे / डाले)।
en: When the flame (arciḥ) flickers (lelāyate) in the well-kindled (samiddhe) fire (havya-vāhane — the carrier of oblations), then one should offer the oblations (āhutīḥ) between the two ājya-bhāgas (ghee-portions).

ws.h: लहराती है / चमकती है / हिलती-डुलती है
ws.e: flickers / licks — intensive (frequentative) of √lī (to cling/lick); describes the dancing, flickering motion of a flame; a vivid sensory image
flame — the visible tongue of fire; from √ṛc (to shine/praise); cognate with 'arc'
well-kindled — sam + iddha (past participle of √indh, to kindle); the fire must be properly lit before offerings are made
the carrier of oblations — havya (that which is offered) + vāhana (carrier); a common epithet for Agni (fire-god), who carries offerings to the gods

ws.h: दो आज्य-भाग / घृत (घी) की दो आहुतियाँ
ws.e: the two ghee-portions — ājya (clarified butter/ghee) + bhāga (portion); two preliminary ghee-oblations offered to Agni and Soma before the main offerings

ws.h: आहुतियाँ / यज्ञ में डाली जाने वाली सामग्री
ws.e: oblations — from ā + √hu (to pour/offer); the substances (ghee, milk, soma, grain) poured into the sacrificial fire

gr: Ritual precision: this mantra describes the correct technique of offering — when the flame is dancing (lelāyate) in the well-kindled fire, place the oblations between the two preliminary ājya-bhāgas (ghee-portions). lelāyate — an intensive (yaṅ-luk) form of √lī, describing the flame's flickering — a vivid image that establishes the sensory beauty of the ritual. The fire is alive, moving, ready to receive. ājya-bhāgau antareṇa — 'between the two ājya-bhāgas': this is a specific ritual rule — the main oblations are inserted between two preliminary ghee-offerings to Agni and Soma. The precision reflects the exactness of Śrauta procedure — every step is prescribed, every moment is timed. The purpose of this detail: the Muṇḍaka is showing the beauty and precision of the ritual system — acknowledging its sophistication before critiquing its ultimate sufficiency.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.2 — The two ājya-bhāgas are preliminary oblations of ghee offered at the beginning of a Vedic sacrifice — one to Agni and one to Soma. The main offerings (āhutīḥ) are then placed between these two. This technical detail comes from the Śrauta Sūtras (e.g., Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.14-15). The intensive form 'lelāyate' is poetically striking — it captures the living, dancing quality of sacrificial fire. The Ṛg Veda frequently describes Agni as 'havya-vāhana' (carrier of oblations) — cf. ṚV 1.1.1: 'agnim īḍe purohitam.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — यह मन्त्र यज्ञ-विधि (ritual procedure) का विशद वर्णन करता है। ज्वाला का 'लेलायते' — अग्नि की जीवन्तता (liveliness) दर्शाता है — यज्ञ सुन्दर और सजीव (alive) है। किन्तु सजीवता = शाश्वतता (eternity) नहीं — यज्ञ अनित्य (impermanent) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says this mantra gives a vivid description of ritual procedure. The flame's 'lelāyate' shows fire's liveliness — the sacrifice is beautiful and alive. But liveliness ≠ eternity — the sacrifice is impermanent.
advaita.ins: The ritual is alive — the fire dances, the ghee sizzles, the mantras ring. It's beautiful. But beauty that flickers is not the same as truth that endures. The flame dances for an hour; the Imperishable endures forever.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — अग्नि = भगवान् का मुख (mouth of the Lord) — 'अहं हि सर्वयज्ञानां भोक्ता' (गीता 9.24)। जब अग्नि प्रज्ज्वलित (समिद्ध) होती है — तब भगवान् आहुति स्वीकार करने को तत्पर हैं। विधिवत् आहुति = भगवान् की सेवा (service to the Lord)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says fire = the mouth of the Lord — 'I am the enjoyer and Lord of all sacrifices' (Gītā 9.24). When the fire is well-kindled, the Lord is ready to accept offerings. Proper oblation = service to the Lord.
vishisht.ins: The dancing flame is God's open hand, ready to receive your offering. The ritual is not just mechanics — it's a meeting. You bring ghee and grain; God brings presence. When the flame dances, the meeting has begun.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'लेलायते अर्चिः' = चेतना की ज्वाला (flame of consciousness) जब जागृत (awakened) होती है — तब आन्तरिक आहुति (inner offering) का सही समय है। बाह्य अग्नि = आन्तरिक अग्नि (inner fire / tapas) का प्रतीक।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'lelāyate arciḥ' = when the flame of consciousness is awakened — that is the right time for inner offering. External fire = symbol of the inner fire (tapas).
aurobindo.ins: The flickering flame outside mirrors a flame inside you — the flame of aspiration, of tapas, of awakened consciousness. When that inner flame dances, pour your offering into it: attention, surrender, will. The outer ritual is the rehearsal; the inner ritual is the performance.

dp.q: 🔍 The beauty and precision of Vedic ritual
dp.a: This mantra is remarkable for its sensory vividness: 'lelāyate arciḥ' — the flame flickers, dances, licks. The intensive (frequentative) form 'lelāyate' captures the ceaseless, rhythmic movement of fire — a living, breathing entity, not a static object. The Vedic ritualist sees fire as alive — Agni is a god, a messenger, a carrier. The ritual sequence: (1) Kindle the fire properly (samiddhe). (2) Wait for the flame to dance (lelāyate arciḥ). (3) Offer the two ājya-bhāgas (preliminary ghee-portions — one to Agni, one to Soma). (4) Between these two, offer the main āhutīḥ (oblations). Why such precision? Vedic ritual is a technology — it operates on the principle that specific actions performed in specific sequences produce specific results. The timing matters (when the flame dances), the sequence matters (between the two ājya-bhāgas), and the material matters (ghee, grain, soma). Like any technology, it works only when operated correctly. The Muṇḍaka's point: the ritual is precise, beautiful, and effective. But precisely because it is a technology, it has limits. A technology produces results within its domain — but it cannot transcend its domain. Fire can cook food and carry offerings; it cannot reveal the Imperishable.

dp.q: 🔍 Agni as havya-vāhana (carrier of oblations)
dp.a: Agni (fire) is called havya-vāhana — 'the carrier of oblations' — because of his unique role in Vedic cosmology: The mediator: Agni stands between the human world and the divine world. When a priest pours ghee into the fire, Agni 'carries' (vahati) the offering up to the gods in heaven. He is the postal service of the cosmos — transforming physical substances (ghee, grain) into subtle offerings that the gods can receive. Ṛg Vedic precedent: the very first verse of the Ṛg Veda (1.1.1) invokes Agni: 'agnim īḍe purohitaṁ yajñasya devam ṛtvijam / hotāraṁ ratnadhātamam' — 'I praise Agni, the household priest, the divine minister of the sacrifice, the invoker, the bestower of treasures.' The multiple Agnis: Vedic tradition recognises multiple forms of Agni: (1) Cosmic Agni — the fire that animates the universe. (2) Ritual Agni — the sacrificial fire that carries offerings. (3) Digestive Agni (Vaiśvānara) — the fire in the belly that digests food. (4) Lightning — Agni in the sky. All are aspects of one principle: the transformative, mediating fire that converts one form of reality into another.

ro: yasya · agnihotram · adarśam · apaurṇamāsam · acāturmāsyam · anāgrayaṇam · atithi-varjitaṁ · ca · ahutam · avaiśvadevam · avidhinā · hutam · ā-saptamān · tasya · lokān · hinasti ||
hi: जिसका अग्निहोत्र दर्श (अमावस्या यज्ञ) रहित है, पौर्णमास (पूर्णिमा यज्ञ) रहित है, चातुर्मास्य (चार-मासी यज्ञ) रहित है, आग्रयण (प्रथम-फसल यज्ञ) रहित है, अतिथि-वर्जित (बिना अतिथि-सेवा का) है, आहुति-रहित (अहुतम्) है, वैश्वदेव-रहित है, और अविधि से (incorrectly) हवन किया गया है — वह (दोषपूर्ण कर्म) उसके सात लोकों (ā-saptamān lokān) को नष्ट (हिनस्ति) कर देता है।
en: He whose agnihotra (daily fire-offering) is without the new-moon rite (adarśa), without the full-moon rite (apaurṇamāsa), without the four-monthly rite (acāturmāsya), without the first-harvest rite (anāgrayaṇa), without hospitality to guests (atithi-varjita), without oblation (ahuta), without the vaiśvadeva offering (avaiśvadeva), or performed incorrectly (avidhinā huta) — such defective ritual destroys his seven worlds (ā-saptamān lokān hinasti).

ws.e: the agnihotra — the daily morning-and-evening fire-offering; the most fundamental Vedic ritual, performed by every initiated householder without fail
without the new-moon rite — a (without) + darśa (new-moon sacrifice); the darśa-pūrṇamāsa is a fortnightly pair of rituals
the four-monthly rite — performed three times a year at the junctures of the three seasons (vaiśva-deva, varuṇa-praghāsa, sāka-medha)
the first-harvest rite — a sacrifice performed when the first grain of the season is harvested; offering the first-fruits to the gods
without hospitality to guests — atithi (guest) + varjita (excluded); hospitality is a sacred duty integral to the sacrificial life
seven worlds — the seven cosmic realms (bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, mahaḥ, janaḥ, tapaḥ, satyam); defective ritual destroys access to all seven

gr: The consequences of defective ritual: this mantra lists eight ways a ritual can be defective (missing components or incorrect performance) and warns that such defective ritual destroys the performer's seven worlds. Eight defects: (1) adarśa — no new-moon rite, (2) apaurṇamāsa — no full-moon rite, (3) acāturmāsya — no four-monthly rite, (4) anāgrayaṇa — no first-harvest rite, (5) atithi-varjita — no guest-hospitality, (6) ahuta — no oblation offered, (7) avaiśvadeva — no vaiśvadeva offering, (8) avidhinā huta — offered incorrectly. ā-saptamān lokān hinasti — 'destroys his seven worlds': the seven worlds are the seven cosmic planes (bhūḥ through satyam). Defective ritual does not merely fail to produce merit — it actively destroys the performer's claim to all seven worlds. The Muṇḍaka's rhetorical point: the ritual system is so demanding and so unforgiving that even a small deficiency can destroy everything. This sets up the critique: a path with such extreme fragility — where one missing component ruins the whole enterprise — cannot be the ultimate path.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.3 — The list of rituals (darśa-pūrṇamāsa, cāturmāsya, āgrayaṇa, vaiśvadeva) comes from the Śrauta and Gṛhya Sūtra traditions. The 'seven worlds' (sapta lokāḥ) are enumerated in various texts — the standard list from the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka is bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, mahaḥ, janaḥ, tapaḥ, satyam. The severity of the warning ('destroys seven worlds') reflects the Brāhmaṇa-era emphasis on ritual exactness — cf. the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa's numerous warnings about the consequences of ritual errors.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — यह मन्त्र दिखाता है कि कर्मकाण्ड कितना कठिन (demanding) और भंगुर (fragile) है — एक भी अंग छूटने से सात लोक नष्ट। ऐसा भंगुर मार्ग अन्तिम मार्ग (ultimate path) कैसे हो सकता है?
advaita.en: Shankara says this mantra shows how demanding and fragile karma-kāṇḍa is — even one missing component destroys seven worlds. Such a fragile path cannot be the ultimate path.
advaita.ins: One missed step and seven worlds fall. That's the ritual path — powerful but brittle. Like a bridge made of glass: beautiful, effective, but one crack and it shatters. The Imperishable, by contrast, cannot crack.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — दोषपूर्ण कर्म = भगवान् की अपमानजनक (disrespectful) सेवा — अतः फल नष्ट होता है। किन्तु यह कर्म-मात्र की निन्दा नहीं — दोषपूर्ण कर्म की निन्दा है। भक्तिपूर्ण और विधिवत् कर्म सार्थक है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says defective ritual = disrespectful service to the Lord — hence the fruit is destroyed. But this is not a condemnation of karma itself — only of defective karma. Devotional and properly performed karma is meaningful.
vishisht.ins: If you invite a king to dinner and then serve the food cold, on a dirty plate, with half the courses missing — would the king be pleased? Ritual is service. Half-hearted service is worse than no service — it insults the one you're serving.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — आठ दोष = चेतना की अपूर्णता (incompleteness of consciousness)। 'सात लोक नष्ट' = चेतना के सातों स्तरों (seven planes of consciousness) पर हानि। अधूरा अभ्यास (incomplete practice) = अधूरा परिणाम (incomplete result)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says eight defects = incompleteness of consciousness. 'Seven worlds destroyed' = loss across all seven planes of consciousness. Incomplete practice = incomplete result.
aurobindo.ins: Half a bridge takes you nowhere — it takes you to the middle of the river, where you drown. The ritual path demands completeness. Miss one piece and the whole structure collapses. That's not a design flaw — it's a warning: mechanical repetition without fullness is worse than not starting.

dp.q: 🔍 The fragility of the ritual system
dp.a: This mantra reveals a critical characteristic of the Vedic ritual path: its extreme fragility: Eight ways to fail: the mantra lists eight specific deficiencies — any one of which 'destroys seven worlds.' This means the ritual path demands perfect compliance: every component must be present, every procedure must be correct. The agnihotra ecosystem: the daily agnihotra is not a standalone practice — it exists within an ecosystem of rituals: new-moon rites (fortnightly), full-moon rites (fortnightly), four-monthly rites (three per year), first-harvest rites (annual), guest-hospitality (ongoing), and vaiśvadeva offerings (daily). Miss any one of these supporting rituals, and the entire edifice collapses. Why such severity? The Brāhmaṇa texts (especially the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa) are filled with similar warnings. The logic is: a sacrifice is a cosmic mechanism — it operates on precise cause-and-effect principles. Like a machine, if one gear is missing, the machine doesn't just produce less — it breaks. The Muṇḍaka's implicit argument: any path that can be destroyed by a single missing component is inherently unstable. It depends on conditions (a functioning fire, correct procedure, proper timing, guest-presence). The Imperishable (akṣara), by contrast, is unconditional — it depends on nothing. This contrast prepares the reader for the explicit critique in mantras 7-13.

dp.q: 🔍 The seven worlds (sapta lokāḥ)
dp.a: The seven worlds (sapta lokāḥ) are the seven cosmic planes of existence in Vedic cosmology: Standard enumeration (from the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka and other texts): (1) Bhūḥ — the earth-plane (physical world). (2) Bhuvaḥ — the atmosphere-plane (intermediate world). (3) Svaḥ — the heaven-plane (celestial world). (4) Mahaḥ — the plane of greatness. (5) Janaḥ — the plane of beings (creative plane). (6) Tapaḥ — the plane of austerity. (7) Satyam — the plane of truth (highest). Connection to the Gāyatrī: the first three (bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ) are the three vyāhṛtis — the sacred utterances chanted with the Gāyatrī mantra every morning and evening. They represent the three basic divisions of the cosmos. 'Destroys seven worlds': defective ritual doesn't just fail to gain heaven — it actively destroys the performer's connection to all seven planes. This is a strong claim: incorrect performance is worse than non-performance. It's better to not sacrifice than to sacrifice badly.

sk: काली कराली च मनोजवा च सुलोहिता या च सुधूम्रवर्णा स्फुलिङ्गिनी विश्वरुची च देवी लेलायमाना इति सप्त जिह्वाः ||
ro: kālī · karālī · ca · mano-javā · ca · sulohitā · yā · ca · sudhūmra-varṇā · sphuliṅginī · viśva-rucī · ca · devī · lelāyamānā · iti · sapta · jihvāḥ ||
hi: काली (black), कराली (terrifying), मनोजवा (swift-as-mind), सुलोहिता (deep-red), सुधूम्रवर्णा (smoky-purple), स्फुलिङ्गिनी (spark-showering), और विश्वरुची देवी (all-gleaming goddess) — ये लेलायमाना (flickering) अग्नि की सात जिह्वाएँ (seven tongues) हैं।
en: Kālī (the black), Karālī (the terrifying), Manojvā (swift-as-mind), Sulohitā (the deep-red), Sudhūmravarṇā (the smoky-purple), Sphuliṅginī (the spark-scattering), and Viśvarucī Devī (the all-gleaming goddess) — these seven flickering (lelāyamānā) tongues are the seven tongues (sapta jihvāḥ) of fire.

ws.e: the black one — the dark-coloured tongue of fire; the first of the seven; kālī = feminine of kāla (black/time)
the terrifying one — from karāla (fearful/gaping); the fierce, gaping flame

ws.h: मन की गति वाली / मन जैसी तेज़
ws.e: swift-as-mind — manas (mind) + java (speed); a flame that moves as fast as thought
the deep-red one — su (very) + lohita (red); the intensely crimson flame
the spark-scattering one — from sphuliṅga (spark); the flame that throws off sparks

ws.h: सर्व-दीप्तिमती देवी / सब ओर चमकने वाली
ws.e: the all-gleaming goddess — viśva (all) + ruci (lustre) + devī (goddess); the flame of universal brilliance
flickering — intensive present participle of √lī; the same word-root as 'lelāyate' in mantra 2; describes the continuous dancing motion of flames

gr: The seven tongues of fire: a striking poetic catalogue of fire's seven 'tongues' (jihvāḥ) — each named for a distinct quality of flame. The names: (1) Kālī (black), (2) Karālī (terrifying), (3) Manojvā (mind-swift), (4) Sulohitā (deep-red), (5) Sudhūmravarṇā (smoky-purple), (6) Sphuliṅginī (spark-scattering), (7) Viśvarucī Devī (all-gleaming goddess). These names are not arbitrary — they describe the actual visual qualities of fire: the dark base, the fearsome roar, the speed, the red core, the smoky edges, the flying sparks, and the universal brilliance. lelāyamānā — 'flickering': connects back to mantra 2's 'lelāyate' — the fire's tongue-like licking motion. Seven as a sacred number: the seven tongues correspond to the seven worlds (mantra 3), seven metres, seven priests, seven continents — 'seven' is a number of cosmic completeness in Vedic thought.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.4 — The seven tongues of fire also appear in a variant form in other texts. This list has some overlap with names found in the Atharvaveda hymns to Agni and in later Purāṇic descriptions of fire's forms. The naming convention reveals close observation of actual fire — the black at the base (kālī), the deep-red core (sulohitā), the smoky edges (sudhūmravarṇā), the sparks (sphuliṅginī), and the all-pervading glow (viśvarucī). The feminine gender of all seven names personifies the flames as goddesses — Agni's śaktis (powers). The next mantra will explain how to use these seven tongues in ritual.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — सात जिह्वाएँ = अग्नि की सात शक्तियाँ (powers) — जो विभिन्न आहुतियों (oblations) को विभिन्न देवताओं तक ले जाती हैं। यह कर्मकाण्ड की विस्तृत (elaborate) जटिलता (complexity) को दर्शाता है — कितना विशाल (vast) तन्त्र (system) — फिर भी यह सब अपरा विद्या है।
advaita.en: Shankara says seven tongues = seven powers of fire — each carries different oblations to different deities. This shows the elaborate complexity of karma-kāṇḍa — how vast the system is — yet all of it is aparā vidyā.
advaita.ins: Seven tongues, seven worlds, seven metres, seven priests — the ritual system is as vast and intricate as the universe it mirrors. And all of it — every tongue, every world, every mantra — is aparā. Beautiful, complex, effective — and still not the final answer.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — सात जिह्वाएँ = भगवान् की सात शक्तियाँ जो यज्ञ में प्रकट होती हैं। प्रत्येक ज्वाला = भगवान् का एक रूप। अग्नि-पूजा = भगवान् की बहु-रूप (multi-form) उपासना।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says seven tongues = seven powers of the Lord manifested in the sacrifice. Each flame = one form of the Lord. Fire-worship = multi-form worship of the Lord.
vishisht.ins: God doesn't show up in fire as one face — He shows up as seven. Black, red, swift, terrifying, sparkling, smoky, radiant. Each tongue is a mood of the divine: fierce grace, swift mercy, burning truth. The ritual is a meeting with all seven.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — सात जिह्वाएँ = चेतना की सात ऊर्जाएँ (seven energies of consciousness) — अग्नि (fire) = परिवर्तनकारी शक्ति (transformative force)। काली = अचेतन (subconscient), विश्वरुची = अतिचेतन (superconscient) — सातों = चेतना का पूर्ण स्पेक्ट्रम।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says seven tongues = seven energies of consciousness — fire = the transformative force. Kālī = subconscient, Viśvarucī = superconscient — all seven = the full spectrum of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Each flame is a frequency of consciousness: from the dark base (the subconscient) through the red core (vital energy) to the all-gleaming summit (the superconscient). The outer fire is a map of the inner fire — seven tongues, seven levels of transformation.

dp.q: 🔍 The seven tongues of fire — poetry meets observation
dp.a: The seven names of fire's tongues are a remarkable fusion of poetic imagination and close empirical observation of actual fire: Physical observation: (1) Kālī (black) — the dark, unburned zone at the base of a flame where fuel is still converting to gas. (2) Karālī (terrifying) — the fierce, roaring aspect of large fires. (3) Manojvā (mind-swift) — the incredible speed with which flames move and spread. (4) Sulohitā (deep-red) — the red-orange core of the flame where combustion is most intense. (5) Sudhūmravarṇā (smoky-purple) — the purplish-grey edges where smoke and flame mix. (6) Sphuliṅginī (spark-scattering) — the flying sparks thrown off by burning wood. (7) Viśvarucī (all-gleaming) — the overall radiance that illuminates everything around it. Mythological layer: the seven tongues are also the seven śaktis (feminine powers) of Agni — each responsible for carrying specific types of offerings to specific deities. The feminine gender of all seven names (ending in ī/ā) reinforces this: they are goddesses, not just physical phenomena. Symbolic layer: the progression from Kālī (black/dark) to Viśvarucī (all-gleaming) mirrors the journey from darkness (ignorance) to light (knowledge) — the central metaphor of all Upanishadic teaching.

dp.q: 🔍 Seven as a cosmic number in Vedic thought
dp.a: Seven (sapta) is one of the most sacred numbers in Vedic cosmology, appearing in dozens of contexts: Seven tongues of fire (this mantra). Seven worlds (sapta lokāḥ — mantra 3). Seven metres (sapta chandāṁsi — gāyatrī, triṣṭubh, jagatī, anuṣṭubh, paṅkti, bṛhatī, uṣṇih). Seven priests (sapta ṛtvijah — hotṛ, adhvaryu, udgātṛ, brahman, and three assistants). Seven rivers (sapta sindhavaḥ — the sacred rivers of the Ṛg Vedic landscape). Seven sages (saptarṣi — the seven great seers who form the constellation Ursa Major). Seven horses of the Sun (the Sun-god's chariot is drawn by seven horses, one for each day of the week or each colour of the spectrum). Why seven? The number seven appears to represent cosmic completeness — the full range of a phenomenon. Seven tongues = the complete fire. Seven worlds = the complete cosmos. Seven sages = the complete lineage of wisdom. The recurrence of seven across so many domains suggests that Vedic thinkers perceived a sevenfold structure in reality itself.

sk: एतेषु यश्चरते भ्राजमानेषु यथाकालं चाहुतयो ह्याददायन् तं नयन्त्येताः सूर्यस्य रश्मयो यत्र देवानां पतिरेकोऽधिवासः ||
ro: eteṣu · yaḥ · carate · bhrājamāneṣu · yathā-kālaṁ · ca · āhutayaḥ · hi · ādadāyan · taṁ · nayanti · etāḥ · sūryasya · raśmayaḥ · yatra · devānāṁ · patiḥ · ekaḥ · adhivāsaḥ ||
hi: इन (सात ज्वालाओं में) जो भ्राजमान (blazing) होते हुए यथाकालम् (proper time पर) चरते (कर्म करते) हैं — और आहुतियाँ (offerings) आददायन् (उचित रूप से ग्रहण की जाती हैं) — उसे ये (आहुतियाँ) सूर्य की रश्मियों (किरणों) के रूप में ले जाती हैं — जहाँ देवताओं का एक पति (lord) अधिवास (dwelling) करता है।
en: He who performs (carate) in these blazing (bhrājamāneṣu) [fires] and whose oblations (āhutayaḥ) are properly received (ādadāyan) at the right time (yathā-kālam) — him these [oblations], as rays of the sun (sūryasya raśmayaḥ), lead (nayanti) to where the one lord of the gods (devānāṁ patiḥ) dwells (adhivāsaḥ).

ws.e: in the blazing [fires/flames] — present participle of √bhrāj (to shine/blaze); the fires must be brilliantly lit for the ritual to succeed

ws.h: उचित समय पर / निर्धारित काल में
ws.e: at the proper time — yathā (as/according to) + kāla (time); timing is critical in Vedic ritual — dawn, dusk, new-moon, etc.

ws.h: स्वीकार की जाती हैं / ग्रहण की जाती हैं
ws.e: are received / accepted — from ā + √dā (to give/receive); the oblations are properly accepted by the fire-god
rays of the sun — the oblations transform into sun-rays that carry the performer upward; connects to the devayāna (path of the gods)
lord of the gods — typically identified with Indra or Prajāpati; the ruler of the heavenly realm to which the ritualist ascends

gr: The reward of correct ritual: when all seven flames are blazing, oblations are offered at the correct time, and the fire accepts them — then the offerings, transformed into sun-rays, carry the performer to the dwelling of the lord of the gods. sūryasya raśmayaḥ — 'rays of the sun': the path from earth to heaven follows the sun's rays — this is the devayāna (path of the gods) described in the Chāndogya (5.10.1-2) and Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2.15). devānāṁ patiḥ ekaḥ adhivāsaḥ — 'where the one lord of the gods dwells': the destination is the divine realm — heaven, ruled by the lord of the gods. Note: this is a loka (world) — however exalted — not the Imperishable (akṣara). The ritual path leads to the highest place, but the Imperishable is not a place. The implicit limitation: the ritualist reaches 'the lord of the gods' — a cosmic ruler — not Brahman itself. This is glory, not liberation.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.5 — The imagery of oblations becoming sun-rays that carry the performer to heaven connects to the devayāna (path of the gods) described in the Chāndogya (5.10.1-2) and Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2.15). The 'lord of the gods' (devānāṁ pati) is variously identified with Indra, Prajāpati, or Hiraṇyagarbha depending on the commentator. The concept of the sun's rays as the vehicle of ascent is also found in the Īśā Upanishad (15-16) where the dying person asks the sun to withdraw its rays to reveal the truth within.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'देवानां पतिः' = हिरण्यगर्भ / प्रजापति — ब्रह्मलोक नहीं, सत्यलोक / स्वर्गलोक। 'सूर्य-रश्मि' = देवयान मार्ग (path of the gods)। यह उच्चतम लोक (highest world) है — किन्तु लोक ही है — अक्षर ब्रह्म नहीं। लोक-प्राप्ति ≠ मोक्ष।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'devānāṁ patiḥ' = Hiraṇyagarbha / Prajāpati — not Brahmaloka but the highest heavenly realm. 'Sun-rays' = devayāna (path of the gods). This is the highest world — but still a world — not akṣara Brahman. Attaining a world ≠ liberation.
advaita.ins: The ritual path delivers you to the lord of the gods — a cosmic throne room, the highest address in creation. But it's still an address. The Imperishable has no address. You can be a guest in the grandest house in the universe and still not be free.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'देवानां पतिः' = भगवान् नारायण — किन्तु यहाँ ऐश्वर्य-प्राप्ति (attainment of glory) का वर्णन है, कैवल्य-मोक्ष (absolute liberation) का नहीं। भक्ति-सहित कर्म = भगवत्-प्राप्ति; भक्ति-रहित कर्म = केवल स्वर्ग-प्राप्ति।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'devānāṁ patiḥ' = Lord Nārāyaṇa — but what is described here is attainment of glory, not absolute liberation. Karma with devotion = attainment of the Lord; karma without devotion = mere attainment of heaven.
vishisht.ins: The ritual, done perfectly, carries you on sun-rays to the throne of the Lord of the gods. That's glorious. But there's a difference between visiting the king's court and being the king's beloved. Rituals get you the visit; devotion gets you the relationship.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'सूर्य-रश्मि' = ज्ञान की किरणें (rays of knowledge) — जो चेतना को ऊपर ले जाती हैं। 'देवानां पतिः' = चेतना का उच्चतम अभिव्यक्त स्तर (highest manifested level) — किन्तु अव्यक्त (unmanifest) ब्रह्म नहीं। बाह्य यज्ञ = चेतना को मानसिक स्तर (mental plane) तक ले जा सकता है — आध्यात्मिक (supramental) तक नहीं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'sun-rays' = rays of knowledge that carry consciousness upward. 'Lord of the gods' = the highest manifested level of consciousness — but not the unmanifest Brahman. External sacrifice can elevate consciousness to the mental plane — not to the supramental.
aurobindo.ins: The sun's rays carry you up — to the highest point from which you can still look down. But the Imperishable isn't up — it's everywhere. The ritual path is a ladder; but the destination isn't at the top of any ladder. It's the ground the ladder stands on.

dp.q: 🔍 The devayāna — path of the gods
dp.a: The imagery of sun-rays carrying the ritualist to heaven connects to one of the most important Upanishadic doctrines — the devayāna (path of the gods): Two paths after death (Chāndogya 5.10, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.2): (1) Devayāna (path of the gods) — for those who have performed rituals and tapas with knowledge. The soul passes through: fire → day → bright fortnight → six months of the northern sun → year → sun → moon → lightning → a 'non-human person' (amānava puruṣa) who leads them to Brahman. (2) Pitṛyāna (path of the ancestors) — for those who performed rituals mechanically. The soul passes through: smoke → night → dark fortnight → six months of the southern sun → world of the ancestors → moon → rain → food → birth again. The Muṇḍaka's position: this mantra describes a path similar to the devayāna — sun-rays carry the performer to the 'lord of the gods.' But the Muṇḍaka will argue (mantras 7-13) that even this glorious path is insufficient because: (a) it leads to a world (however exalted), not to the Imperishable; (b) any world is impermanent — the performer eventually returns. Only parā vidyā leads to the akṣara, from which there is no return.

dp.q: 🔍 Ritual timing — 'yathā-kālam' (at the proper time)
dp.a: The phrase yathā-kālam ('at the proper time') highlights a fundamental principle of Vedic ritual — timing is everything: Why timing matters: Vedic ritual is synchronised with cosmic rhythms. The right action at the wrong time is as ineffective as the wrong action at the right time. Key ritual timings: (1) Agnihotra — performed at dawn (prātaḥ) and dusk (sāyam) every day without exception. (2) Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa — at each new-moon (darśa) and full-moon (pūrṇamāsa). (3) Cāturmāsya — at the three seasonal junctures (every four months). (4) Āgrayaṇa — at the first harvest of the season. (5) Soma sacrifice — coordinated with specific nakshatras (lunar mansions). The underlying principle: the cosmos has rhythms — daily (sunrise/sunset), monthly (moon phases), seasonal (solstices/equinoxes), annual (harvest). Vedic ritual aligns human action with these cosmic rhythms, creating a resonance between microcosm and macrocosm. When you offer at dawn, you participate in the sun's re-creation of the world. When you offer at the new-moon, you participate in the moon's cycle of death and renewal.

sk: एह्येहीति तमाहुतयः सुवर्चसः सूर्यस्य रश्मिभिर्यजमानं वहन्ति प्रियां वाचमभिवदन्त्योऽर्चयन्त्य एष वः पुण्यः सुकृतो ब्रह्मलोकः ||
ro: ehi · ehi · iti · tam · āhutayaḥ · su-varcasaḥ · sūryasya · raśmibhiḥ · yajamānaṁ · vahanti · priyāṁ · vācam · abhivadantyaḥ · arcayantyaḥ · eṣaḥ · vaḥ · puṇyaḥ · su-kṛtaḥ · brahma-lokaḥ ||
hi: 'आओ, आओ!' (एहि एहि) — ऐसा कहती हुई सुवर्चस् (radiant) आहुतियाँ सूर्य की रश्मियों (किरणों) द्वारा यजमान (sacrificer) को ले जाती (वहन्ति) हैं — प्रिय वाणी (प्रिय वचन) बोलती हुई, अर्चना (praise) करती हुई — 'यह तुम्हारा पुण्य सुकृत ब्रह्मलोक है!'
en: 'Come, come!' (ehi ehi) — so say the radiant (su-varcasaḥ) oblations, carrying (vahanti) the sacrificer (yajamāna) on the rays of the sun (sūryasya raśmibhiḥ), speaking sweet words (priyāṁ vācam abhivadantyaḥ), honouring him (arcanyantyaḥ): 'This is your meritorious (puṇya), well-earned (su-kṛta) world of Brahmā (brahma-loka)!'

ws.e: come, come! — imperative of √i (to come); the personified oblations invite the ritualist to ascend to heaven; a vivid prosopopoeia
radiant / lustrous — su (good/beautiful) + varcas (lustre/splendour); the oblations shine with spiritual power
the sacrificer — the patron who commissions and pays for the sacrifice; from √yaj (to sacrifice)

ws.h: मधुर वचन बोलती हुई / स्वागत करती हुई
ws.e: speaking sweet words — abhi + √vad (to speak toward); the oblations welcome the ritualist with pleasant speech
the world of Brahmā — the highest heavenly realm; note: this is brahma-loka (world of Brahmā, the creator), not Brahman itself; a world, however exalted, is still a world

gr: The climax of the ritual path: the personified oblations — radiant, sweet-voiced — carry the sacrificer on sun-rays to brahma-loka, crying 'Come, come!' This is the highest reward of the ritual path, presented in its most attractive form. Prosopopoeia: the oblations are personified — they speak ('ehi ehi'), they use sweet words (priyāṁ vācam), they honour (arcayantyaḥ). This is a literary device that makes heaven feel personal, welcoming, alive. brahma-lokaḥ — 'world of Brahmā': note carefully — this is the world of Brahmā (the creator-god, masculine), not Brahman (the Absolute, neuter). Even the highest world in creation is still within creation — subject to time, subject to eventual dissolution. The pivot: this mantra represents the peak of the ritual path's promise. The next mantra (7) will begin the devastating critique — revealing that this glorious destination is 'leaky' and impermanent.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.6 — The personification of oblations ('ehi ehi') is a rhetorical device designed to make the ritual reward maximally attractive before the critique begins. The term 'brahma-loka' is deliberately ambiguous — it can mean 'world of Brahmā' (the created deity) or 'world of Brahman' (the Absolute). Shankara consistently reads it here as the world of Brahmā (Hiraṇyagarbha) — a created realm — not the uncreated Brahman. This is crucial: the Muṇḍaka's critique depends on brahma-loka being a world (impermanent) rather than Brahman itself (imperishable). The Chāndogya (8.4.1-3) describes brahma-loka as a realm with lakes and rivers — clearly a 'world' with spatial characteristics.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'एहि एहि' = स्वर्ग का मोहक (seductive) निमन्त्रण। 'ब्रह्मलोक' = हिरण्यगर्भ/ब्रह्मा का लोक — अनित्य (impermanent)। अगला मन्त्र (7) इसी मोह (delusion) को तोड़ेगा — यह सब 'प्लवाः' (leaky boats) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'ehi ehi' = the seductive invitation of heaven. 'Brahma-loka' = the world of Hiraṇyagarbha/Brahmā — impermanent. The next mantra (7) will shatter this delusion — all this is 'plavāḥ' (leaky boats).
advaita.ins: Heaven rolls out the red carpet: 'Come, come!' says the shining welcoming committee. Sweet words, honour, a world of merit. It's the best possible advertisement. And the next mantra is the fine print: 'This expires.'

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'ब्रह्मलोक' = भगवान् के ऐश्वर्यमय लोक (glorious realm) — किन्तु यह केवल भोग (enjoyment) का स्थान है, भक्ति-प्रेम (loving devotion) का नहीं। बिना भक्ति = केवल वैभव (splendour) — भगवान् के साथ सम्बन्ध (relationship) नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'brahma-loka' = the Lord's glorious realm — but this is only a place of enjoyment, not of loving devotion. Without bhakti = mere splendour — no relationship with the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Heaven welcomes you like a five-star hotel: 'Come in! Enjoy!' But a hotel isn't a home. You can have the finest room in the universe and still be a guest. Devotion makes you family. Ritual alone makes you a well-treated visitor.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'एहि एहि' = चेतना के ऊर्ध्व स्तरों (higher planes) का आकर्षण (attraction)। 'ब्रह्मलोक' = मानसिक चेतना का उच्चतम स्तर (highest level of mental consciousness) — किन्तु अतिमानसिक (supramental) चेतना नहीं। बाह्य यज्ञ यहाँ तक ला सकता है — आगे नहीं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'ehi ehi' = the attraction of higher planes of consciousness. 'Brahma-loka' = the highest level of mental consciousness — but not supramental consciousness. External sacrifice can bring you here — no further.
aurobindo.ins: The higher planes call out: 'Come up!' And the ritual lifts you — through the sun's rays — to the highest floor. But it's still a floor. Above all floors is the sky — open, boundless, uncreated. The ritual can't take you into the sky.

dp.q: 🔍 Brahma-loka: the highest world — and why it's not enough
dp.a: Brahma-loka ('the world of Brahmā') is the highest realm in Vedic cosmology — and the Muṇḍaka says even this is insufficient: What brahma-loka is: the realm of Brahmā, the creator-god — the highest 'world' (loka) in the hierarchy of bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ... satyam. It is the ultimate reward of perfectly performed ritual — the best destination a karma-based path can achieve. Why it's not enough: (1) It's a world — it has spatial characteristics, a ruler, inhabitants. Anything with characteristics is finite and impermanent. (2) It's earned — and anything earned can be exhausted. When the merit (puṇya) that sent you there runs out, you return to the cycle of birth and death. (3) It's not Brahman — brahma-loka is the world of Brahmā (the created deity), not Brahman (the uncreated Absolute). Even the creator is within creation. The Gītā's confirmation (8.16): 'ā-brahma-bhuvanāl lokāḥ punar-āvartino 'rjuna' — 'All worlds up to brahma-loka are subject to return, O Arjuna.' Even those who reach the highest world must eventually come back. Only those who attain Brahman itself are free from return.

dp.q: 🔍 The personification of oblations — a rhetorical strategy
dp.a: The personification of oblations (āhutīḥ) in this mantra is a deliberate rhetorical strategy: What happens: the oblations — ghee, milk, grain — are personified as radiant beings who speak sweet words, honour the sacrificer, and carry him to heaven on sun-rays. They cry 'Come, come!' like welcoming hosts. Why this imagery: the Muṇḍaka is presenting the ritual path at its most attractive — its best possible version — before critiquing it. If the critique is to be convincing, it must critique the strongest version of the ritual path, not a straw-man. The contrast with what follows: mantras 1-6 present the ritual path with beauty, precision, and grandeur — dancing flames, seven tongues, sun-rays, 'Come, come!' Then mantras 7-13 demolish this grandeur: 'leaky boats' (plava), 'fools who delight in ritual' (iṣṭa-pūrta-manyamānāḥ), 'the blind led by the blind' (andhenaiva nīyamānāḥ yathāndhāḥ). The contrast is devastating because the Muṇḍaka first showed how beautiful the ritual path is. The lesson: it's not that rituals are ugly or false — they are beautiful and true. But beauty and truth at the phenomenal level are not the same as beauty and truth at the ultimate level.

sk: प्लवा ह्येते अदृढा यज्ञरूपा अष्टादशोक्तमवरं येषु कर्म एतच्छ्रेयो येऽभिनन्दन्ति मूढा जरामृत्युं ते पुनरेवापियन्ति ||
ro: plavāḥ · hi · ete · adṛḍhāḥ · yajña-rūpāḥ · aṣṭādaśa · uktam · avaram · yeṣu · karma · etat · śreyaḥ · ye · abhinandanti · mūḍhāḥ · jarā-mṛtyuṁ · te · punaḥ · eva · api · yanti ||
hi: ये (यज्ञ-रूप कर्म) प्लवाः (leaky boats / टूटी नौकाएँ) हैं, अदृढ (unstable / कमज़ोर) हैं — अठारह (अङ्गों में) जिनमें अवर (lower / inferior) कर्म कहा गया है। जो मूढ (deluded) लोग इसे ही श्रेय (the highest good) मानकर अभिनन्दन (celebrate) करते हैं — वे पुनः (again) जरा-मृत्यु (old age and death) को प्राप्त होते (यन्ति) हैं।
en: These ritual forms (yajña-rūpāḥ) are indeed leaky boats (plavāḥ), unstable (adṛḍhāḥ) — the eighteen [components] in which the lower (avara) karma is described. The deluded (mūḍhāḥ) who celebrate (abhinandanti) this as the highest good (śreyaḥ) — they fall again (punaḥ eva api yanti) into old age and death (jarā-mṛtyu).

ws.e: leaky boats / frail rafts — from √plu (to float); boats that seem to float but are full of holes; they carry you partway but eventually sink — the Muṇḍaka's most famous metaphor for ritual
unstable / not firm — a + dṛḍha (firm); the ritual forms are not solid enough to carry one across the ocean of saṁsāra
the forms of sacrifice — rūpa (form/shape) of yajña (sacrifice); the various ritual configurations
eighteen — the eighteen components of the sacrificial system (variously identified: 16 priests + yajamāna + yajamāna's wife; or 7 types of Soma sacrifice + 7 types of Havis sacrifice + 4 Vedas)
the deluded — from √muh (to be confused); those who mistake the means (ritual) for the end (liberation)
old age and death — jarā (old age) + mṛtyu (death); the twin markers of saṁsāra (the cycle of birth and death)

gr: The devastating critique begins: this is the Muṇḍaka's most famous and most radical mantra — the turning point where the ritual path, so beautifully presented in mantras 1-6, is declared to be 'leaky boats.' plavāḥ adṛḍhāḥ — 'leaky boats, unstable': the metaphor is devastating. A leaky boat seems to float — it appears functional, it carries you for a while — but it cannot take you across the ocean. Midway, it sinks. Similarly, rituals seem to work — they produce results (heaven, merit) — but they cannot carry you across the ocean of saṁsāra. aṣṭādaśa — 'eighteen': the eighteen components of the ritual system. Various identifications exist: (a) sixteen priests + yajamāna + his wife = 18; (b) the eighteen sacrificial procedures listed in various Śrauta texts. mūḍhāḥ — 'the deluded': a harsh word. Those who consider the ritual path to be the highest good (śreyaḥ) are not merely mistaken — they are deluded. The problem is not performing rituals but stopping at rituals — thinking them sufficient. jarā-mṛtyuṁ te punar evāpi yanti — 'they again enter old age and death': the ultimate consequence. The ritualist, despite reaching brahma-loka, eventually returns — to old age, to death, to the cycle. The ritual path is a circle, not a line.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.7 — This is the most cited mantra of the Muṇḍaka, appearing in dozens of Vedāntic texts. The 'leaky boats' (plavāḥ) metaphor was enormously influential — Shankara cites it repeatedly in his commentaries to argue for the superiority of jñāna (knowledge) over karma (action). The 'eighteen' (aṣṭādaśa) has been variously interpreted: Shankara takes it as the 16 ṛtvij (priests) + yajamāna + his wife; other commentators identify it with 18 types of sacrificial procedures. The phrase 'jarā-mṛtyuṁ punar evāpi yanti' echoes the Bhagavad Gītā's (9.21) 'kṣīṇe puṇye martya-lokaṁ viśanti' — 'when their merit is exhausted, they enter the mortal world.' The Kaṭha (1.2.5) uses similar language about the deluded.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'प्लवाः' = यज्ञ-कर्म = जर्जर नावें — जो संसार-सागर (ocean of saṁsāra) पार नहीं करा सकतीं। 'अष्टादश' = सोलह ऋत्विज् + यजमान + पत्नी = 18। 'मूढाः' — जो इन्हें ही श्रेय (summum bonum) मानते हैं — वे पुनः जन्म-मरण-चक्र (cycle of birth and death) में पड़ते हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'plavāḥ' = sacrificial rituals = leaky boats — they cannot carry one across the ocean of saṁsāra. 'Aṣṭādaśa' = 16 priests + sacrificer + wife = 18. 'Mūḍhāḥ' — those who consider rituals as the summum bonum fall back into the cycle of birth and death.
advaita.ins: Leaky boats. That's what the Upanishad calls your elaborate, expensive, perfectly performed rituals. Not false boats — leaky boats. They float for a while. They carry you toward heaven. But halfway across the ocean, water seeps in. And you sink — back into birth, old age, and death.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'मूढाः' = जो केवल कर्म पर निर्भर हैं, भक्ति पर नहीं। 'प्लवाः' = भक्ति-रहित कर्म = जर्जर नाव। भक्ति-सहित कर्म = दृढ (firm) नाव — जो भगवान् तक पहुँचा सकती है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'mūḍhāḥ' = those who rely only on karma, not on bhakti. 'Plavāḥ' = karma without devotion = a leaky boat. Karma WITH devotion = a firm boat — which can reach the Lord.
vishisht.ins: The boat leaks because it's missing something: devotion. Ritual without love for God is like a ship without a hull — it looks impressive on the surface but can't hold water. Add devotion, and the same boat becomes seaworthy.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'प्लवाः अदृढाः' = बाह्य कर्मकाण्ड — चेतना-परिवर्तन (transformation of consciousness) का स्थायी साधन नहीं हो सकता। 'मूढाः' = जो बाह्य अनुष्ठान (outer ritual) को आन्तरिक रूपान्तरण (inner transformation) समझ लेते हैं — वे मोहित (deluded) हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'plavāḥ adṛḍhāḥ' = outer ritualism — it cannot be a lasting means for transformation of consciousness. 'Mūḍhāḥ' = those who mistake outer ritual for inner transformation are deluded.
aurobindo.ins: You can rearrange the furniture of the outer life forever — rituals, disciplines, structures — and never touch the inner reality. The leaky boat is any practice that changes the outside without transforming the inside. The water that seeps in is the unaddressed darkness within.

dp.q: 🔍 'Leaky boats' (plavāḥ) — the Muṇḍaka's most famous metaphor
dp.a: The metaphor of plavāḥ ('leaky boats' or 'frail rafts') is the Muṇḍaka's most famous and most cited image: The metaphor: rituals are compared to boats that seem seaworthy but are full of holes. They appear to work — they carry the ritualist toward heaven, just as a leaky boat carries a passenger partway across a river. But partway is not all the way. The holes let water in, and the boat sinks — the ritualist, despite reaching heaven, eventually falls back into the cycle of birth and death. Why 'leaky,' not 'broken'? A broken boat wouldn't float at all. The Muṇḍaka's point is subtler: the ritual boat does float — it produces real results (merit, heaven). The problem is not that it doesn't work but that it doesn't work permanently. The merit earned through ritual is finite; when it's exhausted, the performer returns to mortal life. What makes the boat leak? The 'holes' are the inherent limitations of karma (action): (1) Every action is finite — it produces a finite result. (2) Every finite result is temporary — it eventually ends. (3) Temporary results cannot produce a permanent state (liberation). The only 'solid' vessel: parā vidyā — the knowledge of the Imperishable — is the only vessel without holes. Because it is not an action (karma) producing a result, but a recognition of what already is. You cannot 'use up' the recognition of your own nature.

dp.q: 🔍 'The deluded' (mūḍhāḥ) — why the Muṇḍaka uses harsh language
dp.a: The Muṇḍaka calls ritualists who consider karma the highest good mūḍhāḥ — 'the deluded/confused': Why so harsh? The term mūḍha (from √muh, to be confused/deluded) is strong — it implies not just ignorance but active self-deception. The Muṇḍaka uses it because: (1) The stakes are high: if you mistake the ritual path for the ultimate path, you spend a lifetime (or many lifetimes) on a path that circles back to its starting point. Delusion at this level is not a minor error — it's a cosmic waste of time. (2) The evidence is available: the Upanishads (which are part of the Vedas!) contain the teaching of parā vidyā. The ritualist who reads only the karma-kāṇḍa (ritual portion) and ignores the jñāna-kāṇḍa (knowledge portion) is like someone who reads a map's legend but not its territory. The information is right there — they're choosing not to look. (3) The comparison with the Kaṭha: the Kaṭha Upanishad (1.2.5) uses identical language: 'avidyāyām antare vartamānāḥ svayaṁ dhīrāḥ paṇḍita-manyamānāḥ / dandramyamāṇāḥ pariyanti mūḍhāḥ andhenaiva nīyamānā yathāndhāḥ' — 'Living in the midst of ignorance, self-wise, thinking themselves learned, the deluded wander about like the blind led by the blind.' The Muṇḍaka's compassion: despite the harsh language, the purpose is compassionate — to shake the reader out of complacency. Better a harsh truth now than a pleasant delusion for eternity.

sk: अविद्यायामन्तरे वर्तमानाः स्वयं धीराः पण्डितंमन्यमानाः दन्द्रम्यमाणाः परियन्ति मूढा अन्धेनैव नीयमाना यथान्धाः ||
ro: avidyāyām · antare · vartamānāḥ · svayaṁ · dhīrāḥ · paṇḍitam-manyamānāḥ · dandramyamāṇāḥ · pariyanti · mūḍhāḥ · andhena · eva · nīyamānāḥ · yathā · andhāḥ ||
hi: अविद्या के बीच में (अन्तरे) वर्तमान (dwelling) — स्वयं को धीर (wise) और पण्डित (learned) मानने वाले (मन्यमानाः) — दन्द्रम्यमाणाः (भटकते हुए / staggering) — मूढ (deluded) लोग घूमते (परियन्ति) रहते हैं — जैसे अन्धे (blind) को अन्धा (blind) ले जाता है (अन्धेनैव नीयमाना यथान्धाः)।
en: Dwelling in the midst of ignorance (avidyāyām antare), yet considering themselves wise (dhīrāḥ) and learned (paṇḍitam-manyamānāḥ), the deluded (mūḍhāḥ) go round and round (pariyanti), staggering (dandramyamāṇāḥ), like the blind led by the blind (andhena eva nīyamānā yathā andhāḥ).

ws.e: in ignorance — a + vidyā (knowledge); not the absence of learning but the absence of parā vidyā; they may be highly educated yet spiritually ignorant
thinking themselves learned — paṇḍita (learned) + manyamāna (considering oneself); the self-deception of intellectual pride; they mistake erudition for wisdom

ws.h: भटकते हुए / लड़खड़ाते हुए / ठोकर खाते हुए
ws.e: staggering / stumbling about — intensive of √dram (to run/wander); implies aimless, directionless movement despite apparent purposefulness

ws.h: चारों ओर घूमते हैं / चक्कर लगाते हैं
ws.e: go round and round — pari + √i (to go); circular motion — they travel far but arrive nowhere; the circle of saṁsāra

ws.s: अन्धेनैव नीयमानाः यथान्धाः (andhena eva nīyamānāḥ yathā andhāḥ)
ws.h: जैसे अन्धे द्वारा अन्धे ले जाये जाते हैं
ws.e: like the blind led by the blind — the most devastating image: teachers without parā vidyā leading students without parā vidyā — both equally lost

gr: The blind leading the blind: one of the most famous verses in all of Indian literature — and one that echoes across world traditions. Three layers of delusion: (1) avidyāyām antare vartamānāḥ — 'dwelling in the midst of ignorance': they live surrounded by ignorance, immersed in it, unable to see beyond it. (2) svayaṁ dhīrāḥ paṇḍitam-manyamānāḥ — 'considering themselves wise and learned': the worst kind of ignorance — the ignorance that thinks it is knowledge. They are not humble seekers but proud scholars who believe they have already arrived. (3) andhena eva nīyamānā yathā andhāḥ — 'like the blind led by the blind': teacher and student are equally blind. The teacher, having only aparā vidyā, leads the student in circles — both believing they are progressing. dandramyamāṇāḥ pariyanti — 'staggering, going round and round': the intensive form (dandramyamāṇāḥ) conveys aimless, lurching movement — they stumble and circle without direction. The paradox: these are not uneducated people — they are 'paṇḍita-manyamānāḥ' (considering themselves learned). They may have mastered the four Vedas, the six Vedāṅgas, and all eighteen components of the ritual system. And yet the Muṇḍaka calls them 'blind.' Their blindness is not lack of information but lack of vision — parā vidyā, the direct seeing of the Imperishable.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.8 — This mantra is virtually identical to Kaṭha Upanishad 1.2.5. The Kaṭha version reads: 'avidyāyām antare vartamānāḥ svayaṁ dhīrāḥ paṇḍita-manyamānāḥ / jaṅghanyamānāḥ pariyanti mūḍhā andhenaiva nīyamānā yathāndhāḥ.' The only significant difference is 'jaṅghanyamānāḥ' (Kaṭha) vs. 'dandramyamāṇāḥ' (Muṇḍaka) — both meaning 'staggering/stumbling.' The 'blind leading the blind' image also appears in the New Testament (Matthew 15:14, Luke 6:39), suggesting a universal human recognition of the danger of self-assured ignorance. The Muṇḍaka's use of 'paṇḍita-manyamānāḥ' (considering themselves learned) is particularly sharp — it targets the educated elite, not the uneducated masses.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'अन्धेनैव नीयमाना यथान्धाः' — यह सबसे भयंकर स्थिति है: गुरु भी अन्ध (blind) — शिष्य भी अन्ध। गुरु के पास केवल अपरा विद्या (ritual knowledge) है — परा विद्या (Brahman-knowledge) नहीं। 'पण्डित-मन्यमानाः' = विद्वत्ता का अहंकार (pride of learning) — सबसे बड़ा अवरोध (obstacle)।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'the blind led by the blind' is the most terrible condition: teacher is blind, student is blind. The teacher has only aparā vidyā (ritual knowledge), not parā vidyā. 'Paṇḍita-manyamānāḥ' = pride of learning — the greatest obstacle.
advaita.ins: The most dangerous ignorance is the one wearing a scholar's robe. You've memorised the Vedas, mastered the rituals, earned the title 'Paṇḍit' — and you're still blind. Worse: you're leading others who trust you. Two sets of blind eyes, one confident stride, one cliff ahead.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'अन्ध' = भक्ति-शून्य (devoid of devotion)। बिना भक्ति — वेद-ज्ञान भी 'अविद्या' है। 'पण्डित-मन्यमानाः' = जो शास्त्र-ज्ञान (scriptural knowledge) को ही पूर्ण मानते हैं — भगवत्-प्रेम (love of God) के बिना।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'blind' = devoid of devotion. Without bhakti, even Vedic knowledge is 'avidyā.' 'Paṇḍita-manyamānāḥ' = those who consider scriptural knowledge complete — without love of God.
vishisht.ins: You can read every line about God and still not know God. The scholar who has memorised all the love letters but never felt love — what does he actually know? Knowledge about God without love for God is a library card, not a relationship.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'अन्धेन नीयमाना यथान्धाः' = बौद्धिक अन्धता (intellectual blindness) — जब मन (mind) ही एकमात्र उपकरण (instrument) माना जाता है। मन = अपरा विद्या का उपकरण। परा विद्या के लिए मन से ऊपर (beyond mind) जाना होगा — अतिमानसिक (supramental) चेतना में।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'blind led by blind' = intellectual blindness — when the mind is considered the only instrument. Mind = the instrument of aparā vidyā. For parā vidyā, one must go beyond mind — into supramental consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The mind is the best blind guide there is — it's confident, articulate, and completely unable to see the light. It can map the darkness in extraordinary detail. But it cannot see the sun. For that, you need a faculty the mind doesn't even know it's missing.

dp.q: 🔍 'The blind led by the blind' — a universal warning
dp.a: The image of 'the blind led by the blind' (andhena eva nīyamānā yathā andhāḥ) is one of the most powerful in world literature: In the Upanishadic context: the 'blind' teacher is one who has mastered aparā vidyā (lower knowledge — Vedas, rituals, grammar) but lacks parā vidyā (higher knowledge — direct realisation of Brahman). Such a teacher can recite every mantra, perform every ritual perfectly, and explain every grammatical rule — but cannot point the student toward the Imperishable because he himself has never seen it. Why 'blind,' not 'ignorant'? A blind person cannot see — it's not a matter of trying harder or studying more. The limitation is in the faculty, not the effort. Similarly, aparā vidyā uses the mind as its instrument — but the Imperishable cannot be known by the mind (it is 'ungraspable' — agrāhya, mantra 1.1.6). A different faculty (direct spiritual perception, jñāna-cakṣu) is needed. The Kaṭha parallel: Kaṭha 1.2.5 is virtually identical — 'jaṅghanyamānāḥ pariyanti mūḍhā andhenaiva nīyamānā yathāndhāḥ.' This shared verse suggests a common Upanishadic tradition of critiquing merely intellectual or ritualistic religion. The self-deception: the most dangerous element is 'paṇḍita-manyamānāḥ' — they think they are learned. They are not humble seekers who know they don't know (like Śaunaka, who asked 'what must I know?'). They are confident experts who believe they already have the answer. This confidence is the deepest blindness.

dp.q: 🔍 Avidyā in the Upanishadic sense
dp.a: The term avidyā ('ignorance') in the Upanishads has a specific and technical meaning quite different from ordinary ignorance: Avidyā ≠ lack of education: the people described as dwelling 'in the midst of avidyā' are highly educated — they consider themselves 'paṇḍita' (learned). Their avidyā is not lack of information but lack of realisation. They know many things about the world but don't know the ground of the world. Avidyā = taking the conditioned for the unconditioned: in Shankara's analysis, avidyā is the fundamental error of superimposition (adhyāsa) — taking what is limited, changing, and mortal for what is unlimited, changeless, and immortal. The ritualist superimposes permanence on impermanent results (heaven, merit) — and so remains trapped. Avidyā includes the Vedas: the Muṇḍaka's radical claim (mantra 1.1.5) is that the four Vedas themselves are aparā vidyā — 'lower knowledge.' If the Vedas are aparā, then mastery of the Vedas, without parā vidyā, is still avidyā. The Īśā Upanishad's warning (9): 'andhaṁ tamaḥ praviśanti ye 'vidyām upāsate / tato bhūya iva te tamo ya u vidyāyāṁ ratāḥ' — 'Into blinding darkness enter those who worship avidyā (ignorance); into still greater darkness, those who are devoted to vidyā (knowledge) alone.' The Īśā makes the even stronger claim that vidyā alone (knowledge without wisdom) is more dangerous than plain ignorance — because it creates false confidence.

sk: अविद्यायां बहुधा वर्तमाना वयं कृतार्था इत्यभिमन्यन्ति बालाः यत्कर्मिणो न प्रवेदयन्ति रागात्तेनातुराः क्षीणलोकाश्च्यवन्ते ||
ro: avidyāyāṁ · bahudhā · vartamānāḥ · vayaṁ · kṛta-arthāḥ · iti · abhimanyanti · bālāḥ · yat · karmiṇaḥ · na · pravedayanti · rāgāt · tena · āturāḥ · kṣīṇa-lokāḥ · cyavante ||
hi: अविद्या में बहुधा (बहुत प्रकार से) वर्तमान (रहते हुए) — बाल (childish / अज्ञानी) लोग मानते (अभिमन्यन्ति) हैं — 'हम कृतार्थ (fulfilled / सफल) हैं!' — क्योंकि कर्मी (ritualists) राग (attachment) के कारण (परम तत्त्व को) नहीं जानते (न प्रवेदयन्ति) — इसलिए आतुर (afflicted / दुःखी) होकर, क्षीणलोक (exhausted merit वाले) होकर, च्यवन्ते (fall / गिर जाते हैं)।
en: Dwelling in ignorance (avidyāyām) in many ways (bahudhā), the childish (bālāḥ) think: 'We have achieved our purpose (kṛta-arthāḥ)!' Because the ritualists (karmiṇaḥ), due to attachment (rāgāt), do not know [the supreme reality] (na pravedayanti) — therefore, afflicted (āturāḥ), with their merit exhausted (kṣīṇa-lokāḥ), they fall (cyavante).

ws.e: the childish / the immature — bāla = child; used metaphorically for those who are spiritually immature, regardless of biological age or intellectual attainment
having achieved one's purpose — kṛta (done) + artha (purpose); they believe they have reached the goal; the premature sense of completion
the ritualists — those devoted exclusively to karma (action/ritual); from √kṛ (to do)
due to attachment — rāga (passion/attachment); attachment to the results of ritual; the emotional investment in heaven and merit

ws.h: क्षीण (exhausted) लोक वाले / जिनके पुण्य-लोक समाप्त हो गये
ws.e: with exhausted worlds/merit — kṣīṇa (depleted) + loka (world/merit); when the accumulated merit runs out, the heavenly reward ends

ws.h: गिर जाते हैं / पतित होते हैं
ws.e: they fall — from √cyu (to fall/drop); they fall from heaven back into the mortal world; the technical term for the end of heavenly tenure

gr: The fall from heaven: this mantra completes the critique by describing what happens after the ritualist reaches heaven — he falls. bālāḥ — 'the childish': an even harsher term than 'mūḍhāḥ' (deluded). These are spiritually immature people — like children who are delighted by a toy without understanding its limitations. kṛta-arthāḥ iti abhimanyanti — 'they think: we have achieved our purpose': the ritualist's great mistake is premature satisfaction. Having reached heaven, he thinks the journey is over. But heaven is a station, not the destination. rāgāt na pravedayanti — 'due to attachment, they do not know': attachment (rāga) to the results of ritual blinds them to the supreme reality. The emotional investment in heaven prevents them from looking beyond heaven. kṣīṇa-lokāḥ cyavante — 'with exhausted merit, they fall': this is the critical point. The merit (puṇya) earned through ritual is finite. Like a bank account that can be spent, the merit eventually runs out. When it does, the soul 'falls' (cyavante) from heaven back into the mortal world — back to birth, old age, and death. The Gītā's echo (9.21): 'te taṁ bhuktvā svarga-lokaṁ viśālaṁ kṣīṇe puṇye martya-lokaṁ viśanti' — 'Having enjoyed the vast heavenly world, when their merit is exhausted, they enter the mortal world.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.9 — The concept of 'kṣīṇa-loka' (exhausted merit) is crucial to the Vedāntic critique of karma. The Bhagavad Gītā (9.20-21) elaborates this idea extensively: 'te taṁ bhuktvā svarga-lokaṁ viśālaṁ kṣīṇe puṇye martya-lokaṁ viśanti / evaṁ trayī-dharmam anuprapannā gatāgataṁ kāma-kāmā labhante' — those who follow the Vedic rituals enjoy heaven, but when merit runs out, they return to the mortal world, and so they come and go (gatāgatam). The term 'cyavante' (they fall) is technically significant — it is the standard term for the soul's descent from heaven when merit is exhausted, found in the Chāndogya (5.10.5-6) and Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2.16).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'क्षीणलोकाः च्यवन्ते' = जब पुण्य (merit) क्षीण (exhausted) हो जाता है — तब स्वर्ग से पतन (fall from heaven)। यह सिद्ध करता है कि कर्म-फल = अनित्य (impermanent)। नित्य फल (permanent result) = केवल ब्रह्म-ज्ञान से।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'kṣīṇa-lokāḥ cyavante' = when merit is exhausted, they fall from heaven. This proves karma-phala (fruit of action) = impermanent. Permanent result = only through Brahman-knowledge.
advaita.ins: You saved up enough merit to buy a ticket to heaven. You arrived, enjoyed the view, stayed a while. Then the ticket expired. That's what karma does — it buys you time in a place. But time runs out. Only knowledge of the Imperishable gives you something that doesn't have an expiry date.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'रागात् न प्रवेदयन्ति' — आसक्ति (attachment) ने उन्हें भगवान् के स्वरूप (true nature) से अन्ध (blind) कर दिया। वे स्वर्ग-सुख में इतने मग्न (absorbed) हैं कि भगवान् को ही भूल गये। 'च्यवन्ते' = भगवान् से विमुख (turned away) होने का परिणाम।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'rāgāt na pravedayanti' — attachment has blinded them to the Lord's true nature. They are so absorbed in heavenly pleasures that they forget the Lord Himself. 'Cyavante' = the consequence of turning away from the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Heaven is so beautiful that you forget why you came. The pleasures are so exquisite that you stop looking for the one who created them. And when the pleasures run out — as all created things must — you fall. Not because God pushed you, but because you were standing on pleasure, not on God.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'बालाः' = चेतना-विकास (evolution of consciousness) में बच्चे — जो तात्कालिक (immediate) परिणामों से सन्तुष्ट हो जाते हैं। 'च्यवन्ते' = चेतना का पतन (fall of consciousness) — जब ऊपर उठाने वाली शक्ति (uplifting force) समाप्त हो जाती है — चेतना अपने पूर्व स्तर पर लौट आती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'bālāḥ' = children in the evolution of consciousness — satisfied with immediate results. 'Cyavante' = fall of consciousness — when the uplifting force is spent, consciousness returns to its former level.
aurobindo.ins: A child thinks a trip to the fair is the greatest thing in the world. The lights! The sounds! The candy! But the fair closes. And the child goes home — to the same house, the same room, the same ordinary life. Heaven is the cosmic fair. The Imperishable is your actual home.

dp.q: 🔍 The exhaustion of merit (kṣīṇa-loka) and the fall from heaven
dp.a: The concept of kṣīṇa-loka — 'exhausted worlds/merit' — is central to the Vedāntic critique of karma: How merit works: in the Vedic worldview, good actions (puṇya-karma) generate merit — a kind of spiritual currency that 'buys' a sojourn in heaven. The more elaborate and correct the ritual, the more merit is generated, and the longer the heavenly stay. Why merit runs out: merit is a finite quantity — it was produced by a finite action performed in finite time. A finite cause cannot produce an infinite effect. Therefore, the heavenly reward is proportional to the merit — and when the merit is 'spent,' the reward ends. The fall (cyavana): the standard Upanishadic and later literature describes the soul's 'fall' from heaven as a natural process — not a punishment but a consequence. The Chāndogya (5.10.5-6) describes the descent: 'They return through the same stages: from the moon to ākāśa, from ākāśa to wind, from wind to smoke, from smoke to cloud, from cloud to rain, from rain to earth, from earth to food, from food to seed, from seed to a womb.' The Gītā (9.21) says: 'Having enjoyed the vast heavenly world, when their merit is exhausted, they enter the mortal world. Thus, following the three-Veda dharma, desiring pleasures, they obtain coming-and-going (gatāgatam).' The critique's logic: any path whose reward is proportional to effort cannot lead to permanent liberation. Only a path whose 'result' is the recognition of what already is (rather than the production of something new) can be permanent. Brahman-knowledge doesn't create anything — it reveals what was always there. That's why it can't be exhausted.

dp.q: 🔍 'Bālāḥ' (the childish) — spiritual immaturity vs. intellectual achievement
dp.a: The Muṇḍaka's use of bālāḥ ('the childish') highlights a crucial distinction between intellectual achievement and spiritual maturity: Who are the 'bālāḥ'? These are not uneducated people. The previous mantra called them 'paṇḍita-manyamānāḥ' — those who consider themselves learned. They may have mastered the Vedas, performed elaborate sacrifices, and earned the respect of society. Yet the Muṇḍaka calls them 'bālāḥ' — spiritually childish. Why 'childish'? A child is characterised by: (1) Short time-horizon: attracted to immediate rewards (candy, toys) without considering long-term consequences. The ritualist is attracted to heaven (the cosmic 'candy') without considering that it's temporary. (2) Literalism: takes things at face value without looking for deeper meaning. The ritualist performs rituals literally without seeking their inner significance. (3) Premature satisfaction: thinks the toy IS the happiness, rather than understanding that happiness comes from within. The ritualist thinks heaven IS liberation, rather than understanding that liberation transcends all worlds. The path to maturity: the Muṇḍaka's cure for spiritual immaturity is not more rituals but a different kind of knowledge — parā vidyā. The shift from aparā to parā is the shift from spiritual childhood to spiritual adulthood: from 'what can I get?' to 'what am I?'

sk: इष्टापूर्तं मन्यमाना वरिष्ठं नान्यच्छ्रेयो वेदयन्ते प्रमूढाः नाकस्य पृष्ठे ते सुकृतेऽनुभूत्वेमं लोकं हीनतरं वा विशन्ति ||
ro: iṣṭā-pūrtaṁ · manyamānāḥ · variṣṭhaṁ · na · anyat · śreyaḥ · vedayante · pramūḍhāḥ · nākasya · pṛṣṭhe · te · sukṛte · anubhūtvā · imaṁ · lokaṁ · hīnataraṁ · vā · viśanti ||
hi: इष्टापूर्त (यज्ञ और दान-कर्म) को वरिष्ठ (the best) मानते हुए — प्रमूढ (deeply deluded) लोग — अन्य कोई श्रेय (higher good) नहीं जानते (वेदयन्ते)। नाक (heaven) के पृष्ठ (summit) पर सुकृत (merit) का अनुभव (anubhūtvā) करके — वे इस लोक (this world) में — या इससे भी हीनतर (lower) लोक में — प्रवेश (विशन्ति) करते हैं।
en: Considering iṣṭā-pūrta (sacrifice and charitable works) to be the best (variṣṭham), the deeply deluded (pramūḍhāḥ) know no other higher good (śreyaḥ). Having enjoyed [their merit] (anubhūtvā) on the summit (pṛṣṭhe) of heaven (nākasya), they enter (viśanti) this world — or an even lower one (hīnataram).

ws.e: sacrifice and charitable works — iṣṭa (what is offered in sacrifice) + pūrta (what is done as charity — building wells, temples, tanks); the two categories of meritorious action
the best / the highest — superlative of vara (excellent); they consider ritual and charity as the absolute best one can do
deeply deluded — pra (intensely) + mūḍha (confused); a stronger form of mūḍha (mantra 7); intensely, profoundly confused
on the summit of heaven — nāka (heaven, lit. 'where there is no pain') + pṛṣṭha (back/surface/summit); the very peak of the heavenly realm

ws.h: और भी निम्न / और भी नीचे
ws.e: even lower — comparative of hīna (inferior/low); they may not just return to the human world but could fall even lower — animal or lower births

gr: The complete cycle of the ritualist: rise to heaven's summit → enjoy → merit exhausts → fall to this world or lower. iṣṭā-pūrtam — 'sacrifice and charitable works': iṣṭa = Vedic sacrifices (yajña); pūrta = charitable/public works (building wells, temples, feeding the poor). Together, they represent the complete range of meritorious activity. Even this — the best possible karma — is insufficient. pramūḍhāḥ — 'deeply deluded': even stronger than mūḍhāḥ (mantra 7) — the prefix pra- intensifies. They are not slightly confused but profoundly, deeply deluded. nākasya pṛṣṭhe — 'on the summit of heaven': nāka (literally 'painless-place') = heaven. They reach the very peak of heaven — the highest point possible through karma — and then fall. hīnataram vā viśanti — 'or enter an even lower [world]': the descent may go below the human realm — to animal or lower births. This is the worst-case scenario: not just a return to human life but a regression.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.10 — The term 'iṣṭā-pūrta' is a standard compound in Vedic literature for the two categories of meritorious action: iṣṭa (sacrifice) and pūrta (charity/public works). The Taittirīya Upanishad (1.9.1) and the Dharma Sūtras elaborate on both categories. The phrase 'nākasya pṛṣṭhe' also appears in the Ṛg Veda (1.125.5). The warning about falling to 'hīnataram' (an even lower world) goes beyond the standard 'return to mortal life' — it suggests that exhausted heavenly merit might even lead to sub-human births, a concept more fully developed in the Bhagavad Gītā (16.19-20) and Purāṇic literature.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'इष्टापूर्त' = यज्ञ और दान — कर्म का सर्वश्रेष्ठ रूप — फिर भी अनित्य (impermanent)। 'हीनतरं वा विशन्ति' — स्वर्ग से पतन केवल मनुष्यलोक में नहीं — पशु-योनि (animal birth) में भी हो सकता है। कर्म = चक्र (cycle) — उत्थान और पतन।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'iṣṭā-pūrta' = sacrifice and charity — the highest form of karma — yet still impermanent. 'Hīnataram vā viśanti' — the fall from heaven is not just to the human world — it can be to animal births. Karma = cycle — rise and fall.
advaita.ins: You rise to the very top — the summit of heaven, the peak of merit. And then you fall. Not just back to where you started, but possibly lower. That's the cruelty of the cycle: the higher you climb on merit, the further you can fall when the merit runs out.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'इष्टापूर्त' = अच्छे कर्म — किन्तु भक्ति के बिना ये केवल पुण्य-संचय (merit-accumulation) हैं। पुण्य = बैंक-बैलेन्स — खर्च होता है, समाप्त होता है। भक्ति = भगवान् से सम्बन्ध (relationship with God) — जो कभी समाप्त नहीं होता।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'iṣṭā-pūrta' = good deeds — but without devotion, these are merely merit-accumulation. Merit = bank-balance — it can be spent and exhausted. Bhakti = relationship with God — which never expires.
vishisht.ins: Sacrifice and charity fill your merit-account. A full account gets you the best room in heaven. But accounts run dry. What never runs dry? Love. Love for God doesn't deplete — it deepens. That's why bhakti outlasts all the merit in the universe.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'नाकस्य पृष्ठे' = चेतना के उच्चतम मानसिक स्तर (highest mental plane) पर — जहाँ बाह्य कर्म ले जा सकता है। किन्तु बिना आन्तरिक रूपान्तरण (inner transformation) — चेतना पुनः नीचे गिरती है — गुरुत्वाकर्षण (gravity) की तरह।
