aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'nākasya pṛṣṭhe' = the highest mental plane — where external action can take you. But without inner transformation, consciousness falls back down — like gravity.
aurobindo.ins: You can throw a ball as high as you like — it still comes down. That's what karma does: it throws your consciousness upward. But without transformation, gravity wins. The only way to stay up is to become light itself — not to be thrown but to rise by your own nature.

dp.q: 🔍 Iṣṭā-pūrta — the two categories of meritorious action
dp.a: Iṣṭā-pūrta (इष्टापूर्त) is a standard Vedic compound for the two categories of meritorious action: Iṣṭa (इष्ट) — 'what is offered': refers to Vedic sacrifices (yajña) — the formal, fire-based rituals described in the Śrauta and Gṛhya Sūtras. Examples: agnihotra, darśa-pūrṇamāsa, soma sacrifice, aśvamedha. These are 'iṣṭa' because they involve offering (iṣ/yaj) substances into fire. Pūrta (पूर्त) — 'what is completed/fulfilled': refers to charitable and public works — actions that benefit the community. Examples: digging wells, building tanks, planting trees, constructing temples, feeding the poor. These are 'pūrta' because they 'complete' or 'fulfil' a social need. Together: iṣṭā-pūrta represents the complete range of good karma — both religious (sacrifice) and social (charity). The Muṇḍaka's point is devastating: even this — the best possible karma, both sacred and social — is insufficient for liberation. It produces merit that eventually exhausts.

dp.q: 🔍 'Hīnataram vā viśanti' — the possibility of regression
dp.a: The phrase 'hīnataram vā viśanti' ('or they enter an even lower [world]') introduces a frightening possibility: not just return to the human world but regression to a lower one: What 'lower' means: the standard hierarchy of births places gods at the top, then humans, then animals, then plants, then inanimate matter. A 'hīnatara' (more inferior) world would mean an animal or lower birth — not just a return to human status but an actual descent. Why regression is possible: (1) The soul that reaches heaven through karma develops strong saṁskāras (habitual patterns) of enjoyment. (2) When heaven ends, these enjoyment-patterns don't disappear — they persist. (3) The soul, driven by these patterns, seeks the kind of enjoyment it became accustomed to — and may take a birth suited to that enjoyment rather than one suited to spiritual progress. (4) A soul accustomed to heavenly pleasure may not have the discipline for human spiritual life — and so may take a 'lower' birth where pleasure-seeking dominates. The Gītā's parallel (16.19-20): 'Those who are hateful, cruel, the lowest of humans — I cast them into demonic wombs. Entering demonic wombs, the deluded, birth after birth not reaching Me, fall to the lowest state.' While this Gītā passage deals with a different context (the demoniac nature), the principle is similar: consciousness shaped by wrong values descends rather than ascends.

sk: तपःश्रद्धे ये ह्युपवसन्त्यरण्ये शान्ता विद्वांसो भैक्ष्यचर्यां चरन्तः सूर्यद्वारेण ते विरजाः प्रयान्ति यत्रामृतः स पुरुषो ह्यव्ययात्मा ||
ro: tapaḥ-śraddhe · ye · hi · upavasanti · araṇye · śāntāḥ · vidvāṁsaḥ · bhaikṣya-caryāṁ · carantaḥ · sūrya-dvāreṇa · te · virajāḥ · prayānti · yatra · amṛtaḥ · saḥ · puruṣaḥ · hi · avyaya-ātmā ||
hi: जो तपस् (austerity) और श्रद्धा (faith) में अरण्य (forest) में उपवसन्ति (dwell / रहते हैं) — शान्त (peaceful), विद्वान् (learned/wise), भैक्ष्यचर्या (life of alms / भिक्षा-वृत्ति) चरते हुए — वे विरज (passionless / pure) होकर सूर्यद्वार (sun-gate) से प्रयान्ति (depart / जाते हैं) — जहाँ वह अमृत (immortal) पुरुष (Person) है — अव्ययात्मा (the imperishable Self)।
en: Those who dwell (upavasanti) in the forest (araṇye) in austerity (tapas) and faith (śraddhā), peaceful (śāntāḥ), wise (vidvāṁsaḥ), living on alms (bhaikṣya-caryām carantaḥ) — they, passionless (virajāḥ), depart through the sun-gate (sūrya-dvāreṇa) to where that immortal (amṛtaḥ) Person (puruṣa) is — the imperishable Self (avyaya-ātmā).

ws.e: in austerity and faith — tapas (spiritual heat/discipline) + śraddhā (faith/trust); the two pillars of the contemplative life; tapas = inner fire, śraddhā = trust in the teaching
in the forest — the place of retreat, away from society; the setting for the āraṇyaka ('forest texts') and Upanishads
the life of alms — bhaikṣya (alms/begging) + caryā (conduct/practice); the renunciant's practice of living on whatever food is freely offered

ws.h: सूर्य-द्वार से / सूर्य के मार्ग से
ws.e: through the sun-gate — sūrya (sun) + dvāra (door/gate); the doorway through which the liberated soul departs; the devayāna (path of the gods) reaches its culmination at the sun
passionless / pure — vi + rajas (passion/dust); free from all rajas (passion, attachment, desire); having transcended the guṇas
the imperishable Self — avyaya (undecaying) + ātman (Self); the ultimate reality that never changes, never diminishes, never perishes

gr: The alternative path: having devastated the ritual path (mantras 7-10), the Muṇḍaka now presents the alternative — the path of knowledge, austerity, faith, and renunciation. The contrast: ritualists perform sacrifices → reach heaven → fall back. Contemplatives dwell in forests with tapas and śraddhā → depart through the sun-gate → reach the immortal, imperishable Self → never return. Five qualities of the contemplative: (1) tapas — austerity/spiritual discipline, (2) śraddhā — faith/trust, (3) śānta — peaceful, (4) vidvāṁsa — wise/learned (with parā vidyā), (5) bhaikṣya-caryā — living on alms. sūrya-dvāreṇa — 'through the sun-gate': the devayāna path reaches its climax at the sun — the doorway between the created world and the uncreated. The liberated soul passes through the sun into the realm of the Imperishable. avyaya-ātmā — 'the imperishable Self': the destination is not a world (loka) but the Self (ātman) — which is imperishable (avyaya). This is the crucial difference: the ritualist goes to a place; the contemplative goes to what he already is.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.11 — The 'sūrya-dvāra' (sun-gate) connects to the devayāna (path of the gods) described in the Chāndogya (5.10.1-2) and Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2.15). The Chāndogya (8.6.5) also mentions the sun as the gateway: 'atha yad u caivāsmāc charīrād utkrāmati athaitair eva raśmibhir ūrdhvam ākramate' — 'When he departs from this body, he ascends upward by these very rays.' The emphasis on tapas + śraddhā echoes the Taittirīya (2.4.1): 'vijñānaṁ ca tapaś ca' — 'knowledge and austerity together.' The term 'virajāḥ' (passionless) recurs in the Muṇḍaka (3.1.3) and is a key concept in the sannyāsa tradition.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'अरण्ये उपवसन्ति' = संन्यास (renunciation) — कर्मकाण्ड का त्याग। 'सूर्यद्वारेण' = देवयान मार्ग — किन्तु यहाँ 'क्रम-मुक्ति' (gradual liberation) का वर्णन है। सर्वोच्च (highest) = तत्काल मुक्ति (immediate liberation) — 'ब्रह्म वेद ब्रह्मैव भवति' (3.2.9)।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'araṇye upavasanti' = renunciation — abandoning ritual. 'Sūrya-dvāreṇa' = the devayāna path — but this describes 'krama-mukti' (gradual liberation). The highest = immediate liberation — 'the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman' (3.2.9).
advaita.ins: There are two ways out: the gradual path (through the sun-gate, step by step) and the direct path (recognise Brahman here and now). This mantra describes the gradual path — beautiful, valid, but still a journey. The direct path has no journey: you're already there.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'तपः-श्रद्धे' = भक्ति-पूर्ण साधना (devotion-filled practice)। 'अव्ययात्मा पुरुषः' = भगवान् नारायण — जो अमृत (immortal) और अव्यय (imperishable) हैं। 'सूर्यद्वार' = अर्चिरादि मार्ग (archirādi mārga) — भक्त भगवान् के धाम (abode) में प्रवेश करता है — और कभी लौटता नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'tapaḥ-śraddhe' = devotion-filled practice. 'Avyaya-ātmā puruṣa' = Lord Nārāyaṇa — immortal and imperishable. 'Sūrya-dvāra' = the archirādi path — the devotee enters the Lord's abode and never returns.
vishisht.ins: The devotee doesn't fall because he doesn't go to a place — he goes to a Person. You can exhaust a place; you cannot exhaust a Person. When you reach the imperishable Self through the sun-gate, you've come home — and home doesn't have an expiry date.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'अरण्ये' = बाह्य एकान्त (outer solitude) + आन्तरिक शान्ति (inner silence)। 'सूर्यद्वारेण' = चेतना सूर्य-तत्त्व (supramental sun) से होकर अव्यय आत्मा (imperishable Self) में प्रवेश करती है — यह रूपान्तरण (transformation), न कि केवल उत्थान (ascent) है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'araṇye' = outer solitude + inner silence. 'Sūrya-dvāreṇa' = consciousness passes through the supramental sun into the imperishable Self — this is transformation, not merely ascent.
aurobindo.ins: The forest is where you go to hear yourself think — and then to go beyond thinking. In the silence, with austerity as your fire and faith as your fuel, you burn through the layers of self-deception. Through the sun-gate of truth, you enter what you always were: the imperishable Self.

dp.q: 🔍 The sun-gate (sūrya-dvāra) — the exit from creation
dp.a: The sūrya-dvāra ('sun-gate') is one of the most important images in Upanishadic eschatology — the doorway through which the liberated soul exits creation: The devayāna culmination: the devayāna (path of the gods) described in the Chāndogya (5.10.1-2) and Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2.15) passes through several stages: fire → day → bright fortnight → six months of the northern sun → year → the sun → moon → lightning → a non-human person (amānava puruṣa) → Brahman. The sun is the critical gateway — the boundary between the created cosmos and the uncreated Absolute. The Chāndogya's sun-gate (8.6.5): 'When he departs from this body, he ascends upward by these very rays [of the sun]... The sun is the gate of the world [of Brahman]. Those who know enter; those who don't know are turned back.' The Īśā Upanishad's sun-prayer (15-16): 'The face of truth is covered by a golden disc. Remove it, O sun, so that I — the lover of truth — may see [the truth within].' The sun simultaneously reveals (by its light) and conceals (by its dazzling brilliance) the truth beyond. Why the sun? The sun is the most luminous object in creation — it illuminates everything else. But beyond the sun is a light that illuminates even the sun. The sun-gate is the threshold between created light and uncreated Light.

dp.q: 🔍 Tapas and śraddhā — the twin pillars of the contemplative path
dp.a: The Muṇḍaka names tapas (austerity) and śraddhā (faith) as the two foundations of the contemplative life: Tapas (तपस्): literally 'heat' — the spiritual heat generated by discipline, concentration, and self-restraint. Tapas is not mere self-mortification but the inner fire that burns away impurities: (1) Physical tapas: fasting, silence, endurance of hardship. (2) Mental tapas: concentration, one-pointed focus, withdrawal from distractions. (3) Spiritual tapas: the burning desire for truth that consumes all lesser desires. Tapas is what Brahman itself used to create the world (Muṇḍaka 1.1.8: 'tapasā cīyate brahma'). The contemplative mirrors the Creator's method. Śraddhā (श्रद्धा): not 'belief' in the Western sense but trust — trust in the teaching, trust in the teacher, trust in the process. Śraddhā is what keeps the seeker going when results are not yet visible: (1) Trust in the Upanishadic teaching: that brahma-vidyā is real and attainable. (2) Trust in the guru: that the teacher has seen what he teaches. (3) Trust in the process: that tapas, meditation, and inquiry will yield results. Together: tapas without śraddhā becomes dry self-punishment. Śraddhā without tapas becomes wishful thinking. The two together create the conditions for parā vidyā — the direct realisation of the Imperishable.

sk: परीक्ष्य लोकान्कर्मचितान्ब्राह्मणो निर्वेदमायान्नास्त्यकृतः कृतेन तद्विज्ञानार्थं स गुरुमेवाभिगच्छेत्समित्पाणिः श्रोत्रियं ब्रह्मनिष्ठम् ||
ro: parīkṣya · lokān · karma-citān · brāhmaṇaḥ · nirvedam · āyāt · na · asti · akṛtaḥ · kṛtena · tat · vijñāna-arthaṁ · saḥ · gurum · eva · abhigacchet · samit-pāṇiḥ · śrotriyaṁ · brahma-niṣṭham ||
hi: कर्म-चित (karma-built) लोकों को परीक्ष्य (examining / जाँच करके) — ब्राह्मण (seeker of Brahman) को निर्वेद (dispassion / वैराग्य) आना चाहिए — 'अकृत (the uncreated / unproduced) कृत (the produced / created) से नहीं है (नास्ति)' — उस (ब्रह्म के) विज्ञान (realisation) के अर्थ (for the sake of) — वह समित्पाणि (fuel-in-hand) होकर गुरु के पास ही अभिगच्छेत् (approach / जाये) — जो श्रोत्रिय (Veda-learned) और ब्रह्मनिष्ठ (established in Brahman) हो।
en: Having examined (parīkṣya) the worlds built by karma (karma-citān lokān), the brāhmaṇa (seeker of Brahman) should arrive at dispassion (nirvedam āyāt): 'The uncreated (akṛtaḥ) is not [attained] by the created (kṛtena).' For the sake of that knowledge (tad vijñāna-artham), he should approach (abhigacchet) a guru — fuel in hand (samit-pāṇiḥ) — one who is learned in scripture (śrotriya) and established in Brahman (brahma-niṣṭha).

ws.e: having examined / having critically investigated — pari + √īkṣ (to see/examine); not blind rejection but thoughtful examination of karma's results

ws.h: कर्म से निर्मित / कर्म से संचित
ws.e: built by karma / accumulated through action — karma + cita (built/accumulated); the worlds (heavens) are constructed by the merit of ritual action — and therefore impermanent
dispassion / disenchantment — nir + veda (from √vid, to know); literally 'knowing thoroughly' → disillusionment; not depression but clear-eyed recognition that karma-built worlds are insufficient

ws.h: समिधा (ईंधन / sacrificial fuel) हाथ में लिये हुए
ws.e: with fuel-sticks in hand — samidh (sacrificial fuel) + pāṇi (hand); the traditional sign of a student approaching a teacher; carrying fuel signifies readiness to serve and learn
learned in scripture — one who knows the śruti (Vedic texts) thoroughly; from śrotra (hearing); the guru must know the texts
established in Brahman — brahman + niṣṭha (established/grounded); the guru must not only know the texts but be personally established in the direct experience of Brahman

gr: The turning point — from ritual to knowledge: this is one of the most important mantras in the Muṇḍaka — it describes the moment of transition from the karma-path to the jñāna-path. parīkṣya lokān karma-citān — 'having examined the karma-built worlds': the transition begins with examination (parīkṣā) — not blind rejection but thoughtful investigation. The seeker examines the results of karma and sees their limitation: they are 'cita' (built/accumulated) — and anything built can be unbuilt. nirvedam āyāt — 'should arrive at dispassion': nirvedā = disenchantment — the clear-eyed recognition that karma-built worlds are insufficient. This is not depression but wisdom — the maturity to seek beyond the familiar. nāsty akṛtaḥ kṛtena — 'the uncreated is not [attained] by the created': this is the logical kernel of the entire critique. The akṛta (uncreated = Brahman) cannot be reached by kṛta (the created = karma and its results). Created means cannot reach an uncreated goal. This principle is the foundation of Vedāntic epistemology. samit-pāṇiḥ — 'fuel in hand': the seeker approaches the guru carrying sacrificial fuel-sticks — a traditional symbol of submission and readiness to serve. śrotriyaṁ brahma-niṣṭham — 'learned in scripture AND established in Brahman': the guru must have both qualifications — textual knowledge (śrotriya) and direct experience (brahma-niṣṭha). Either alone is insufficient.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.12 — This mantra is one of the most cited in the entire Upanishadic corpus. The phrase 'nāsty akṛtaḥ kṛtena' (the uncreated is not attained by the created) is the logical foundation of the jñāna-mārga (path of knowledge). The dual qualification of the guru — 'śrotriya' (Veda-learned) and 'brahma-niṣṭha' (established in Brahman) — is cited by Shankara in his Vivekacūḍāmaṇi and other works as the standard for a qualified guru. The 'samit-pāṇi' (fuel-in-hand) image appears also in the Chāndogya (4.4.5) where Satyakāma approaches Gautama Hāridrumata, and in the Bhagavad Gītā (4.34): 'tad viddhi praṇipātena paripraśnena sevayā' — 'Know that by prostration, inquiry, and service.' The concept of 'nirveda' (dispassion born of examination) is distinct from vairāgya (detachment) — nirveda arises specifically from seeing through the limitations of karma.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'नास्त्यकृतः कृतेन' — यह वेदान्त का मूल सिद्धान्त (fundamental principle) है: अकृत (uncreated) ब्रह्म — कृत (created) कर्म से प्राप्त नहीं। कर्म = ससीम (finite); ब्रह्म = असीम (infinite)। ससीम साधन (finite means) से असीम लक्ष्य (infinite goal) = असम्भव। 'श्रोत्रियं ब्रह्मनिष्ठम्' — गुरु में दोनों गुण अनिवार्य।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'nāsty akṛtaḥ kṛtena' — this is Vedānta's fundamental principle: the uncreated Brahman cannot be attained by created karma. Karma = finite; Brahman = infinite. Finite means cannot reach an infinite goal. 'Śrotriyaṁ brahma-niṣṭham' — both qualities are indispensable in a guru.
advaita.ins: No amount of doing can reach what was never made. That's the key insight: Brahman wasn't produced, so it can't be produced by your efforts. You can only recognise it — and for that, you need a teacher who has both the map (scripture) and the territory (experience).

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'परीक्ष्य' = विवेक (discrimination) — कर्म-फल की अनित्यता (impermanence of karma-results) को देखकर। 'श्रोत्रियं ब्रह्मनिष्ठम्' = गुरु — जो शास्त्र (scripture) और अनुभव (experience) दोनों में प्रतिष्ठित हो — भगवान् का प्रतिनिधि (representative of the Lord)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'parīkṣya' = discrimination — seeing the impermanence of karma-results. 'Śrotriyaṁ brahma-niṣṭham' = a guru established in both scripture and experience — the Lord's representative.
vishisht.ins: First, look carefully at what karma offers — and notice it expires. Then go to someone who has both the knowledge of scripture and the experience of God. Carry fuel in your hand: come as a servant, not a customer. The guru isn't selling; he's transmitting.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'निर्वेद' = बाह्य उपलब्धियों (external achievements) से विरक्ति — चेतना का अन्तर्मुख (inward turn) होना। 'नास्त्यकृतः कृतेन' = बाह्य क्रिया (external action) से आन्तरिक सत्ता (inner being) नहीं बदलती। रूपान्तरण (transformation) = गुरु-कृपा (guru's grace) + आत्म-समर्पण (self-surrender) से।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'nirveda' = disenchantment with external achievements — consciousness turning inward. 'Nāsty akṛtaḥ kṛtena' = external action cannot change inner being. Transformation = guru's grace + self-surrender.
aurobindo.ins: The moment of nirveda is when you realise: everything I've built will fall. Every world I've earned will expire. What remains? Something I didn't build — something uncreated. And to find that, I need a guide who lives in it: a guru who knows the texts AND knows the truth they point to.

dp.q: 🔍 'The uncreated is not attained by the created' (nāsty akṛtaḥ kṛtena)
dp.a: The phrase 'nāsty akṛtaḥ kṛtena' is one of the most important philosophical statements in the Upanishads: The argument: (1) Karma (action/ritual) is kṛta — something that is 'done/made/created.' (2) Its results are also kṛta — 'made/produced' by the action. (3) Brahman is akṛta — 'uncreated/unmade' — it was not produced by anything and does not depend on anything for its existence. (4) Therefore: a created means (karma) cannot reach an uncreated end (Brahman). Why this is decisive: this principle eliminates all action-based paths as ultimate means to liberation — not just Vedic ritual but any activity, practice, or technique that 'produces' a result. If liberation were a 'product,' it would be impermanent (all products are). Liberation must therefore be a recognition of what already is — not a production of something new. The clay-pot revisited: a pot is 'kṛta' (made); clay is 'akṛta' relative to the pot. No amount of pot-making will reveal the clay — you need to see through the pot to the clay. Similarly, no amount of karma will reveal Brahman — you need to see through the world (the 'pot') to Brahman (the 'clay'). The implication for practice: this doesn't mean 'do nothing.' It means: practice (tapas, meditation, inquiry) creates the conditions for recognition — it removes obstacles, quiets the mind, purifies the heart — but the recognition itself is not 'produced' by practice. It dawns by grace, through the guru's teaching, when the conditions are right.

dp.q: 🔍 The qualified guru — śrotriya and brahma-niṣṭha
dp.a: The Muṇḍaka specifies two qualifications for a guru — both are necessary, neither alone is sufficient: Śrotriya (श्रोत्रिय) — 'learned in the śruti (Vedic texts)': the guru must know the texts — the Upanishads, the commentaries, the tradition. This ensures: (1) Accuracy: the teaching is grounded in the authoritative tradition, not in personal opinion. (2) Communicability: the guru can express the truth in words that the student can understand, using the established vocabulary and framework. (3) Protection against error: without textual knowledge, a person might mistake a limited experience for the final truth. Brahma-niṣṭha (ब्रह्मनिष्ठ) — 'established in Brahman': the guru must have directly experienced Brahman — not just read about it. This ensures: (1) Authenticity: the teaching comes from lived experience, not mere book-learning. (2) Transmission: there is a quality of presence in a brahma-niṣṭha guru that no text can replicate. (3) Guidance through obstacles: the guru who has traversed the path can guide the student through difficulties that no text anticipates. Why both? A guru who is śrotriya but not brahma-niṣṭha is a scholar — he can explain the texts but cannot transmit the experience. A guru who is brahma-niṣṭha but not śrotriya may have the experience but cannot communicate it accurately — he might mislead the student through imprecise language. The ideal guru unites textual mastery with experiential realisation.

sk: तस्मै स विद्वानुपसन्नाय सम्यक्प्रशान्तचित्ताय शमान्विताय येनाक्षरं पुरुषं वेद सत्यं प्रोवाच तां तत्त्वतो ब्रह्मविद्याम् ||
ro: tasmai · saḥ · vidvān · upasannāya · samyak · praśānta-cittāya · śama-anvitāya · yena · akṣaraṁ · puruṣaṁ · veda · satyaṁ · provāca · tāṁ · tattvataḥ · brahma-vidyām ||
hi: उस (विद्यार्थी) को — जो विद्वान् (learned) गुरु — जो उपसन्न (duly approached) हो, सम्यक् प्रशान्तचित्त (truly tranquil-minded) हो, शमान्वित (endowed with inner peace) हो — उसे (गुरु) वह तत्त्वतः (in its true nature / यथार्थ रूप में) ब्रह्मविद्या प्रोवाच (taught / कही) — जिससे (येन) अक्षर (Imperishable) पुरुष (Person) को — सत्य (truth) को — जाना (वेद) जाता है।
en: To him — who has duly approached (upasannāya), whose mind is truly tranquil (praśānta-cittāya), who is endowed with inner peace (śama-anvitāya) — that wise [guru] (vidvān) taught (provāca) the brahma-vidyā in its true nature (tattvataḥ) — by which one knows (veda) the Imperishable (akṣara) Person (puruṣa), the Truth (satya).

ws.h: उपसन्न / विधिवत् पास आये हुए (शिष्य) को
ws.e: to the one who has duly approached — upa + √sad (to sit near); the same term used for Śaunaka in 1.1.3; the student who comes with proper attitude and submission
to the one whose mind is truly tranquil — pra + śānta (deeply peaceful) + citta (mind); the student's mind must be still — free from agitation, doubt, and restlessness
endowed with inner peace — śama (tranquillity/self-control) + anvita (endowed with); related to the Vedāntic sādhana-catuṣṭaya (fourfold qualification for a student)

ws.h: तत्त्व से / यथार्थ रूप में / सत्य-स्वरूप में
ws.e: in its true nature / truly — tattva (that-ness / reality) + taḥ (from/by); the teaching is given not superficially but in its essential, true nature
the Imperishable Person — akṣara (imperishable) + puruṣa (person/being); Brahman described as both imperishable and personal — not just an abstract principle but a living reality
the Truth — satya = that which truly IS (sat + ya); the ultimate reality; Brahman is not just imperishable but TRUE — the only thing that fully, unconditionally exists

gr: The closing of the section: the Muṇḍaka's first section ends with the guru teaching brahma-vidyā to the prepared student. Three qualifications of the student: (1) upasanna — duly approached (with humility and proper procedure), (2) praśānta-citta — truly tranquil-minded (mind free from agitation), (3) śama-anvita — endowed with inner peace (self-control, equanimity). The student must be prepared — the teaching cannot be received by an agitated, proud, or restless mind. tattvataḥ — 'in its true nature': the guru teaches not a simplified version, not a watered-down approximation, but the truth itself (tattva). This requires both the guru's qualification (śrotriya and brahma-niṣṭha) and the student's readiness (praśānta-citta and śama-anvita). akṣaraṁ puruṣaṁ satyam — 'the Imperishable Person, the Truth': three descriptions of the same reality — it is akṣara (imperishable), puruṣa (a living being/person, not an abstraction), and satya (truth — what truly is). This mantra bridges the first section (the critique) and the second section (the positive teaching about Brahman that will begin in Mundaka 2).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.2.13 — This closing mantra establishes the framework for the rest of the Muṇḍaka: from here on, the Upanishad will teach brahma-vidyā 'tattvataḥ' (in its true nature). The student qualifications (praśānta-citta, śama-anvita) connect to Shankara's sādhana-catuṣṭaya — the fourfold qualification for a Vedānta student: viveka (discrimination), vairāgya (dispassion), ṣaṭ-sampatti (six virtues starting with śama), and mumukṣutva (desire for liberation). The triple description 'akṣaraṁ puruṣaṁ satyam' anticipates the Muṇḍaka's treatment of Brahman as both impersonal (akṣara) and personal (puruṣa) — a synthesis that influenced both Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita interpretations.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'तत्त्वतः' = यथार्थ रूप में — न कि उपचारिक (figurative) अर्थ में। 'अक्षरं पुरुषं सत्यम्' = निर्गुण ब्रह्म — जो अक्षर (imperishable), पुरुष (conscious being — not material), और सत्य (the only real) है। गुरु केवल अधिकारी (qualified) शिष्य को ही तत्त्वतः ब्रह्मविद्या देता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'tattvataḥ' = in its true nature — not figuratively. 'Akṣaraṁ puruṣaṁ satyam' = nirguṇa Brahman — imperishable, conscious (not material), and the only real. The guru teaches brahma-vidyā tattvataḥ only to a qualified student.
advaita.ins: The teaching has two conditions: the teacher must know, and the student must be ready. Not intellectually ready — spiritually ready. Mind still. Heart peaceful. Ego quiet. Then — and only then — the guru speaks the truth of the Imperishable. And the student hears it — not with the ears but with the being.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'अक्षरं पुरुषं सत्यम्' = भगवान् — जो अक्षर (अविनाशी), पुरुष (सगुण / with attributes / personal), और सत्य (परम सत्य) हैं। ब्रह्मविद्या = भगवान् के सत्य-स्वरूप (true nature) का ज्ञान। गुरु = भगवान् के प्रतिनिधि — भक्ति-ज्ञान के माध्यम (channel)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'akṣaraṁ puruṣaṁ satyam' = the Lord — imperishable, personal (with attributes), and the supreme Truth. Brahma-vidyā = knowledge of the Lord's true nature. The guru = the Lord's representative — a channel for devotion-knowledge.
vishisht.ins: The guru doesn't teach you a theory — he introduces you to a Person. The Imperishable Person, the Truth. Not an abstraction but a living reality with whom you can have a relationship. When the student is ready and the guru speaks — the introduction happens.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'प्रशान्तचित्त' और 'शमान्वित' = चेतना की ग्रहणशीलता (receptivity of consciousness) — जब मन शान्त होता है — तब सत्य अपने आप प्रकट होता है। 'तत्त्वतः' = चेतना-से-चेतना (consciousness-to-consciousness) — शब्दों का नहीं बल्कि सत्ता का संचार (transmission of being)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'praśānta-citta' and 'śama-anvita' = receptivity of consciousness — when the mind is still, truth reveals itself. 'Tattvataḥ' = consciousness-to-consciousness — not a transmission of words but of being.
aurobindo.ins: The guru doesn't pour knowledge into an empty cup — he stills the water until you can see the bottom. When the mind is truly quiet, the truth that was always there becomes visible. The teaching is not information; it's revelation — the removal of what was blocking the view.

dp.q: 🔍 The qualified student — praśānta-citta and śama-anvita
dp.a: The Muṇḍaka specifies three qualifications for the student who can receive brahma-vidyā: (1) Upasanna — 'duly approached': the student must come to the guru with the proper attitude — humility, submission, genuine desire to learn. This is the same term used for Śaunaka in 1.1.3 — 'vidhivat upasannaḥ.' The approach is not casual; it is formal, respectful, and serious. (2) Praśānta-citta — 'truly tranquil-minded': praśānta = deeply peaceful (not just temporarily calm). The mind must be free from: (a) Agitation (vikṣepa) — restlessness, distraction, mental noise. (b) Doubt (saṁśaya) — the wavering between 'is it true?' and 'is it not?' (c) Attachment (āsakti) — clinging to specific outcomes, including the desire for heaven. (3) Śama-anvita — 'endowed with inner peace': śama = self-control, mastery over the senses and emotions. This is the first of the 'six virtues' (ṣaṭ-sampatti) in Shankara's system: śama (control of mind), dama (control of senses), uparati (withdrawal from worldly pursuits), titikṣā (endurance), samādhāna (concentration), śraddhā (faith). Why these qualifications matter: brahma-vidyā cannot be 'received' by an agitated mind, just as a turbulent lake cannot reflect the moon. The teaching is not information that can be absorbed through effort — it is a revelation that dawns when the mind is perfectly still. The guru's words are the occasion; the student's stillness is the condition.

dp.q: 🔍 The triple description: akṣaraṁ puruṣaṁ satyam
dp.a: Brahman is described with three terms — akṣara (imperishable), puruṣa (person), and satya (truth) — each revealing a different aspect: Akṣara (अक्षर) — 'the Imperishable': Brahman does not change, decay, or perish. While everything in the manifest world is kṣara (perishable), Brahman is a-kṣara — beyond change, beyond time. This is Brahman's ontological character. Puruṣa (पुरुष) — 'Person': Brahman is not a dead abstraction or a blind force — it is a conscious being. The word puruṣa (from pur + √śī, 'one who dwells in the city [of the body]') implies sentience, awareness, agency. This is Brahman's conscious character. The use of puruṣa here is significant for Viśiṣṭādvaita — it supports the view that Brahman is personal, not just impersonal. Satya (सत्य) — 'Truth': Brahman is not merely a being among beings but the truth of all beings — the only thing that truly, unconditionally IS. Everything else exists conditionally (depending on time, space, and causation); Brahman exists unconditionally. The Taittirīya (2.1.1) defines Brahman as 'satyaṁ jñānam anantam' — 'truth, knowledge, infinity.' Three-in-one: the Imperishable (it endures), the Person (it is conscious), the Truth (it is real). These three aspects together give a 'stereoscopic' view of Brahman — not flat but dimensional, not abstract but alive.
